title: Wedding Crashers
logline: Owen Wilson and Vince Vaughn crash weddings to meet women. Fast-talking banter comedy.
overview: John and his buddy Jeremy are emotional criminals who know how to use a woman's hopes and dreams for their own carnal gain. Their modus operandi: crashing weddings. Normally, they meet guests who want to toast the romantic day with a random hook-up. But when John meets Claire, he discovers what true love – and heartache – feels like.

jokes.text: Hey, I got an idea. Why don't you just kiss my left nut?
jokes.setup: Two divorcing spouses are screaming over each other about custody, affairs, and character attacks in an escalating mediation session.
jokes.punchline: John (a mediator) cheerfully interjects with a crude non-sequitur as though it's a legitimate conflict-resolution suggestion.
jokes.explanation: Works as a cold-open punchline because the professional framing (mediator) makes the crudeness land harder. The specificity of 'left nut' versus a generic insult adds comedic texture. It's well-timed as an escalation break.

jokes.text: Let's see, that takes us to frequent flyer miles. We're flying!
jokes.setup: John and Jeremy are mediating a bitter divorce. After a screaming match, they pivot to itemized asset division.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy announces 'frequent flyer miles' with the same manic enthusiasm as a game show host, punctuated by 'We're flying!'
jokes.explanation: The mismatched energy — genuine enthusiasm for the most trivial divorce asset — is the joke. Character-specific for Jeremy's manic optimism. Not exceptional but lands cleanly.

jokes.text: Yeah, you earned them flying to Denver to meet your whore.
jokes.setup: Husband insists the frequent flyer miles are his because he earned them.
jokes.punchline: Wife agrees — but specifies he earned them by flying to Denver to visit his mistress.
jokes.explanation: Classic comic agreement-with-a-twist structure. The setup is the word 'earned' and the punchline recontextualizes it perfectly. Tight economy — she needs only one sentence to devastate him.

jokes.text: She is not a whore! / Her name is Chastity! / She is not! / She's a stripper, for God's sake!
jokes.setup: Husband defends his mistress as not a whore.
jokes.punchline: The name 'Chastity' is revealed — an ironic name for a stripper — which the husband then also denies.
jokes.explanation: The name 'Chastity' for a stripper is a sharp, self-contained irony joke. The rapid-fire back-and-forth escalation (not a whore / her name is Chastity / she's a stripper) is well-structured comedy writing. Quotable standalone line.

jokes.text: That's it, go comatose for me, baby.
jokes.setup: The couple has descended into petty name-calling ('hillbilly,' 'white trash').
jokes.punchline: Jeremy mutters 'go comatose for me, baby' as though coaching a client he's given up on, as if catatonia is the ideal outcome.
jokes.explanation: Extremely economical — four words that reveal Jeremy's exhausted professional detachment. The affectionate 'baby' appended to such a dark sentiment is the kicker. Very character-specific.

jokes.text: You shut your mouth when you're talkin' to me!
jokes.setup: John tries to restore order in the increasingly chaotic mediation.
jokes.punchline: The husband blurts an oxymoronic non-sequitur — a logical impossibility delivered in complete earnest.
jokes.explanation: A classic absurdist self-contradiction that's become a pop-culture catchphrase. The joke is entirely structural — the logical impossibility of the phrase. High quotability despite moderate craft.

jokes.text: What'd you have to eat? Crab cakes. Are you kidding me? Crab cakes! How could you not have a good time eating crab cakes?
jokes.setup: John and Jeremy try to redirect the warring couple toward positive wedding memories to defuse the tension.
jokes.punchline: John's over-the-top genuine enthusiasm about crab cakes — as if they're the universal solution to marital discord — becomes the joke.
jokes.explanation: John's character-specific mania for the mundane sells this. The comedic logic — 'how could you fight if you had crab cakes?' — is absurd but delivered with absolute sincerity, which is where the laugh lives.

jokes.text: Who gives a shit? It's a great band, it's a bad band, it's like pizza, baby. It's good no matter what.
jokes.setup: John and Jeremy ask the couple if they had a band at their wedding, implying music is another good memory.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy waves away any possible answer with the pizza analogy — delivered with total conviction.
jokes.explanation: The pizza analogy is a solid piece of Vaughn-style riffing — casual, confident, and character-revealing. 'It's good no matter what' is delivered with the authority of a philosopher, which amplifies the silliness.

jokes.text: Just a couple of kids who like to fuck, trying to make it honest. I get it.
jokes.setup: John and Jeremy wax nostalgic about wedding dancing — 'rubbing up against each other' — in a sincere attempt to reconnect the divorcing couple with their romantic origins.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy reduces the entire romantic ideal of marriage to its bluntest physical terms, delivered with gentle empathy.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the reel. The structure is near-perfect: the buildup through nostalgic wedding imagery makes the brutal reductionism hit harder. 'Trying to make it honest' — three words that contain an entire satirical thesis about marriage. Extremely economical, deeply character-specific for Jeremy's crass-but-oddly-wise persona, and genuinely quotable. This is what an 8+ joke looks like: it's funny AND it says something.

jokes.text: And how about you? Don't you want to get inside Chastity without having to wonder if everyone's gonna find out?
jokes.setup: Jeremy mirrors John's pitch to the wife, now addressing the husband.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy uses 'Chastity' — the stripper/mistress name established earlier — as the natural object of the husband's post-divorce desires, making the irony of the name land a second time.
jokes.explanation: A solid callback to the Chastity name joke that also moves the scene forward. The callback adds value here: it's not just a name-drop, it contextualizes the husband's actual motivation and makes the divorce pitch land comedically.

jokes.text: Put your swords away for a second... Get out there and get some strange ass.
jokes.setup: John and Jeremy are wrapping up their dual pitch to the couple to finalize the divorce.
jokes.punchline: The formal 'put your swords away' idiom is immediately followed by the blunt 'get some strange ass,' collapsing the professional/vulgar register gap.
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of the formal sword metaphor with the crude slang is well-executed. 'Strange ass' as the stated therapeutic goal of divorce mediation is a sharp conceptual joke.

jokes.text: Hey John, that's weird. That glass looks half full to me. / Wow, now that you mention it, it is half full.
jokes.setup: The wife is about to take a pill (presumably a sedative or anxiety medication) with water. The glass of water is implied to be half empty.
jokes.punchline: John and Jeremy exchange an absurdly serene 'glass half full' moment in the middle of this chaos — using it as a genuine optimism metaphor while completely ignoring the ongoing crisis.
jokes.explanation: A quiet but effective beat — the two men having a wholesome philosophical exchange as a woman takes medication during their mediation session. The incongruity is the joke. Modest but charming.

jokes.text: He can have the miles. / Nah, sweetie, you take the miles.
jokes.setup: The entire opening has been a vicious fight over frequent flyer miles among other things.
jokes.punchline: After the medication-assisted breakdown, the couple has a sudden reversal and become sweetly generous about the miles — the exact thing they were fighting about.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback payoff to the miles dispute. The irony of them suddenly being generous after the medication kicks in lands as a commentary on how arbitrary the fighting was. Economy is good — the reversal needs only two lines.

jokes.text: This is just semantics... The big thing is, is that we're all movin' on. / Could you two just not talk anymore?
jokes.setup: Jeremy is waxing philosophical about the resolution as the attorney tries to close out the paperwork.
jokes.punchline: The attorney's flat 'Could you two just not talk anymore?' is the perfect deflation of Jeremy's self-satisfaction.
jokes.explanation: A clean reaction beat. The exhausted attorney voicing what the audience has been thinking is functional comedy — not inventive but executed efficiently.

jokes.text: I sleep over at John's house every year for his birthday. Okay, that's not creepy.
jokes.setup: Jeremy is explaining to Janice why he needs a comforter from the office supply closet.
jokes.punchline: He casually mentions he sleeps over at his adult male best friend's house every year for his birthday — Janice responds with 'that's not creepy' in a way that clearly means it is.
jokes.explanation: The setup-punchline structure is tight. The humor comes from Jeremy's complete obliviousness to how the sleepover sounds, and Janice's diplomatic sarcasm. Sets up the elaborate tragic backstory that follows.

jokes.text: I guess it is a little creepy when a young man who happens to be an only child loses both of his parents in a tragic accident one month before his birthday and then has a best friend make a vow that he will never spend his birthday alone again.
jokes.setup: Janice calls the birthday sleepover 'not creepy' (meaning: it is). Jeremy seems about to agree it's weird.
jokes.punchline: Instead of a quick self-aware quip, Jeremy delivers an enormous, deeply sad elaborate backstory that completely reframes the 'creepy' behavior as profoundly tragic — making Janice feel terrible.
jokes.explanation: Smart misdirection: we expect Jeremy to either confirm the creepiness or give a mundane excuse. Instead, the punchline is a devastating emotional reveal that makes the previous 'joke' retroactively cruel. The structure is excellent — it builds slowly and lands hard. Character-specific in that it establishes Jeremy as someone who weaponizes sincerity.

jokes.text: Jeremy's extended monologue about the horrors of dating — from the food-on-your-face anxiety to 'Just the Tip'
jokes.setup: Janice suggests she has 'the perfect girl' for Jeremy after he guilts her.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy launches into a rapid-fire, exhaustively specific monologue cataloguing every reason dating is terrible — escalating from normal social anxiety ('do I have food on my face?') to sexual negotiation games ('Just the Tip / Ouch Ouch You're on My Hair').
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest comedic set pieces in this reel. The monologue is a showcase for Vaughn's motormouth style and is expertly structured: it starts relatable (food anxiety) and escalates to the absurd ('Just the Tip'), with a detour through the 'ass-out hug' that is precisely observed physical comedy. The 'are we gonna get hopped enough to make some bad decisions' line is a great turning-point. The names 'Just the Tip' and 'Ouch Ouch You're on My Hair' as game titles are genuinely inventive. Scores 8+ because it's exceptional character work: this rant could ONLY come from Jeremy.

jokes.text: Just for a second, just to see how it feels, or 'Ouch Ouch, You're on My Hair.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy describes the game 'Just the Tip' as a sexual negotiation.
jokes.punchline: He adds a second game: 'Ouch Ouch, You're on My Hair' — a comically specific, anatomically awkward scenario that escalates the riff into full absurdism.
jokes.explanation: The specific name 'Ouch Ouch, You're on My Hair' is comic genius in miniature. It implies a whole scenario without explaining it, it's uncomfortable, it's specific, and the rhythm of the phrase is funny on its own. High originality for coining a named sex game that became a cultural reference point for this film. Near-perfect economy.

jokes.text: Okay. Okay, can... can you... can you put that so he... he can't see it? And thank you. Hey, Janice. Great talk.
jokes.setup: Jeremy has just named 'Ouch Ouch You're on My Hair' as a sex game to his secretary.
jokes.punchline: He immediately becomes self-conscious about the visual aid (presumably a photo of the blind date), dismisses the entire conversation with 'Great talk,' and exits — the deflation of his own energy.
jokes.explanation: 'Great talk' as a button on a conversation that was entirely inappropriate is a solid, well-timed exit joke. The hiding of the photo and the stammer sells that Jeremy knows he went too far, but his breezy exit denies it.

jokes.text: It's wedding season, kid! You sandbagging son of a bitch!
jokes.setup: John asks Jeremy what's so urgent. Jeremy has been building up to a reveal.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy announces 'wedding season' with messianic ecstasy; John's reaction — 'you sandbagging son of a bitch' — is a term of pure affection and excitement, treating wedding crashing like a beloved sport.
jokes.explanation: This is the film's thesis statement delivered as a comedy beat. 'You sandbagging son of a bitch' as a joyful greeting is an excellent comedic inversion — a pejorative becomes an embrace. High character integration: this is exactly who John is.

jokes.text: Now, how many of 'em are cash bars? Great question, love where your head's at, and two of them actually are. But... I got us covered. Purple hearts. We won't have to pay for a drink all night.
jokes.setup: Jeremy describes 17 upcoming weddings and John's first question is about cash bars.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy has preemptively procured military decorations (Purple Hearts) to fraudulently get free drinks at cash-bar weddings — revealing the depth of their planning and moral flexibility.
jokes.explanation: The Purple Hearts detail is excellent worldbuilding comedy — it establishes the characters' willingness to go further than expected and their elaborate preparation. 'Love where your head's at' for asking about cash bars is a great character moment for Jeremy.

jokes.text: Grab that net and catch that beautiful butterfly, pal!
jokes.setup: Jeremy is describing the opportunity at weddings: women aroused by the idea of marriage will 'throw their inhibitions to the wind.'
jokes.punchline: The butterfly metaphor for sex-seeking women, delivered with complete earnestness and poetic gusto by Jeremy, is absurdly grandiose.
jokes.explanation: Jeremy's rhetorical flights are a consistent comic device. The butterfly image for a predatory romantic pursuit is a funny incongruity. Not the strongest of these riffs but functional.

jokes.text: What do you like better? Christmas or wedding season? / The answer would be... wedding season?
jokes.setup: Jeremy asks a rhetorical question framing wedding season as equivalent to Christmas.
jokes.punchline: John, the supposedly reluctant one, answers 'wedding season' with barely disguised eagerness despite just being the voice of caution.
jokes.explanation: A clean character beat — John pretends to be the reluctant one but his answer reveals he loves this as much as Jeremy. The 'Bingo' response from Jeremy is a satisfying button.

jokes.text: Hey, Lou Epstein, I want you to meet a real mensch, Chuck Schwartz.
jokes.setup: John and Jeremy arrive at the first wedding having invented Jewish aliases.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy introduces 'John' as 'Chuck Schwartz' with a Yiddish honorific — the performative Jewishness of two obvious gentile wedding crashers playing characters.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the contrast between who these men clearly are and the total conviction of their cover. 'Real mensch' delivered as natural small talk is the core of the joke. The names (Lou Epstein, Chuck Schwartz, Sanjay Collins, etc.) will pay off across the montage.

jokes.text: Does anyone know what this here is used for? / Rolling a fatty.
jokes.setup: During the Jewish wedding reception, Jeremy picks up some kind of implement (likely a cake/pastry tool) and asks who knows what it's for — presumably expecting no one to know.
jokes.punchline: A child at the wedding immediately answers 'Rolling a fatty' (rolling a marijuana cigarette).
jokes.explanation: Classic innocence-corrupted joke structure — a child knowing something they shouldn't know. The economy is near-perfect: three words is all it takes. The surprise is entirely in the gap between the innocent ask and the drug-reference answer.

jokes.text: You both look beautiful up there today, particularly Debbie in that white dress. Enjoy it. After tomorrow, I don't think you're gonna be able to get away with wearing a white dress.
jokes.setup: Jeremy is chatting up the bride and groom, ostensibly complimenting them.
jokes.punchline: His toast implies the bride is not, or will not remain, 'pure' — delivered with a warm smile as though it's a compliment.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed back-handed compliment that pivots from genuine sweetness to implied insult. The delivery — 'Enjoy it' as a soft warning — is what sells it. Character-specific for Jeremy's brazen social obliviousness.

jokes.text: In the words of the old country... L'chaim! / L'chaim!
jokes.setup: Two obvious gentiles are deep in their Jewish wedding cover personas.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy invokes 'the old country' — as if he has generational connection to this — before toasting with 'L'chaim,' and John eagerly echoes it.
jokes.explanation: A light, functional joke — 'the old country' is doing a lot of work for someone who clearly has no old country. Part of the ongoing wedding-crashing identity comedy but not a standout within it.

jokes.text: I want you to take this note, bring it to that blonde girl. Hurry, 'cause I'm gonna time you. Go!
jokes.setup: In the middle of the reception festivities, John spots a woman.
jokes.punchline: John sends a note via a child messenger and times him — treating a child like a human delivery service with military urgency, which is both absurd and reveals his single-minded romantic opportunism.
jokes.explanation: 'I'm gonna time you' applied to a child messenger on a romantic errand is a funny deployment of competitive urgency. Reveals John's character efficiently.

jokes.text: Now you probably think I'm a big pussy. / No, you were so sweet. Come here.
jokes.setup: The woman caught John watching her cry at the ceremony. John tries to manage her perception of him.
jokes.punchline: His self-deprecating preempt ('you probably think I'm a big pussy') actually charms her — she pulls him in physically.
jokes.explanation: Light charm comedy. The joke is that his self-undermining actually works — a standard comedic reversal. Not especially inventive but pleasant.

jokes.text: Look, I knew I was never gonna be a professional bullfighter, but that's not why I did it. / Weren't you scared? / Can I say yes?
jokes.setup: John is apparently in the middle of an elaborate false backstory about bullfighting.
jokes.punchline: His pivot — 'Can I say yes?' — reveals he's aware his own fiction has become uncomfortable, breaking the fourth wall of the lie slightly.
jokes.explanation: 'Can I say yes?' is a beautifully compressed moment of self-awareness within a lie — John doesn't break character, he just quietly signals he knows this is absurd. The bullfighting backstory as a seduction gambit is already funny, but this line elevates it. Very economical.

jokes.text: Sanjay Collins / Chuck Vindaloo, excited to be here. / Shamus O'Toole / Bobby O'Shea. And we're gonna get drunk.
jokes.setup: The wedding montage shows John and Jeremy introducing themselves at various weddings with invented ethnic cover names.
jokes.punchline: The names escalate in absurdity (Chuck Vindaloo — a curry dish — for an Indian wedding; Bobby O'Shea for Irish), culminating in one introduction where the man's only platform is 'we're gonna get drunk.'
jokes.explanation: The running gag of absurd ethnic aliases is well-executed across the montage. 'Chuck Vindaloo' is the standout — naming yourself after an Indian dish at an Indian wedding is brilliantly stupid. 'And we're gonna get drunk' as an introduction is a great deflation of the alias game.

jokes.text: Uh, I think that's his kid Leonard. The diabetic. / That's Luigi and Gina's son Christopher. You know, the banker. / Oh, that's Mae Lin's adopted son Benny, the veterinarian.
jokes.setup: John and Jeremy survey attractive women at the reception and ask each other who they are.
jokes.punchline: Instead of the men pointing out women, they're identifying other men — apparently knowing the family structures of the weddings they've crashed in extreme, unnecessary detail.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that these crashers have done such deep reconnaissance they know every minor family member's professional life. The specificity ('the diabetic,' 'the banker,' 'the veterinarian') is what makes it funny rather than just a character noting. Reveals the absurd depth of their preparation.

jokes.text: The French Foreign Legion? / Yeah. We lost a lot of good men out there.
jokes.setup: During the wedding montage, someone questions one of their cover stories.
jokes.punchline: The crasher invokes the French Foreign Legion cover story and immediately deploys the 'we lost a lot of good men' line.
jokes.explanation: The 'we lost a lot of good men' line is a perfect all-purpose sympathy gambit — it works for literally any dangerous scenario. The montage then explicitly repeats it for Mount Everest and playing for the Yankees, which turns it into a running gag.

jokes.text: Mount Everest? / I just don't like to talk about it because we lost so many good men out there. / Playing with the Yankees? / Yes, with the Yankees. You lose good men to trades and unruly fans.
jokes.setup: The 'we lost a lot of good men' line from the Foreign Legion exchange.
jokes.punchline: The same line is redeployed for Mount Everest (fine) and then absurdly for the Yankees — 'you lose good men to trades and unruly fans' — the deflation of the military/tragedy register into baseball bureaucracy.
jokes.explanation: The Yankees escalation is where this running gag earns its score. The first two iterations (Foreign Legion, Everest) are good setups, but applying 'lost so many good men' to baseball trades is a perfectly absurd deflation — the pathos of genuine loss applied to being traded from the Yankees is genuinely funny writing. 'Unruly fans' as a cause of casualty is a great specific detail. This is the best iteration of the gag and it's well-structured as a callback escalation.

jokes.text: Tattoo on the lower back. Might as well be a bull's-eye.
jokes.setup: During the wedding montage, Jeremy surveys potential targets.
jokes.punchline: The 'tramp stamp' — lower back tattoo — is reframed as a targeting reticle for sexual pursuit, delivered with casual authority.
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the film and a cultural catchphrase. Near-perfect economy — eight words that land a complete comedic image. The metaphor is vivid, the delivery is deadpan, and the character voice is unmistakable. Loses points on earned_vs_cheap as it trades on existing cultural shorthand about lower back tattoos.

jokes.text: You know how they say we only use 10% of our brains? I think we only use 10% of our hearts.
jokes.setup: John is delivering a seduction line to a woman at a wedding.
jokes.punchline: He takes the well-known pop-science myth about brain usage and replaces 'brains' with 'hearts' — a pseudo-profound non-sequitur delivered as genuine romantic wisdom.
jokes.explanation: A deceptively sharp joke. The structure is a perfect parody of seduction-speak — it uses the form of a 'deep thought' to say something that sounds profound but is completely meaningless. The fact that it presumably WORKS on the recipient makes it funnier. Very economical. High quotability because it sounds like a real thing someone would say unironically.

jokes.text: I feel so tiny in your arms. / Really? How tall are you? / I'm 6'5", but... I feel like I'm four feet. / And some poetry, courtesy of Sarah McLachlan.
jokes.setup: A woman delivers a classic romantic line: 'I feel so tiny in your arms.'
jokes.punchline: John's pragmatic follow-up reveals she is 6'5" — undercutting the romance entirely — and Jeremy's aside 'courtesy of Sarah McLachlan' frames the moment as cheesy movie-of-the-week sentiment.
jokes.explanation: Two-stage joke with both parts landing. First the visual/logical subversion (she's 6'5" but feels tiny) followed by Jeremy's perfectly timed 'courtesy of Sarah McLachlan' — a meta-commentary that skewers the romantic cliché while keeping us on the crashers' side. The Sarah McLachlan tag is the stronger element: it name-drops without being a cheap reference, using the association to do satirical work.

jokes.text: Let's go, let's make a memory! / What are you gonna do for an encore? Walk on water?
jokes.setup: Jeremy is at the center of the wedding party's energy during 'Shout' — the life of the reception.
jokes.punchline: A guest compares Jeremy to a messianic figure — 'walk on water' — as a compliment, which is a funny overcalibration of the praise.
jokes.explanation: A light background joke during the montage. The messianic hyperbole is mild comedy — the joke exists but doesn't earn more than a chuckle.

jokes.text: You want that cake! You don't treat cake like that. You gotta treat cake like a lady.
jokes.setup: During the reception montage, Jeremy apparently intervenes in someone's interaction with wedding cake.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy applies romantic/chivalric codes ('treat her like a lady') to a piece of cake — the category error is the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'Treat cake like a lady' is an economical absurdist moment — applying romantic etiquette to dessert. The image of Jeremy solemnly instructing someone on the proper treatment of wedding cake is very funny. Quotable as a standalone.

jokes.text: And then everyone said, 'Jabroni!'
jokes.setup: Jeremy is mid-anecdote during the reception.
jokes.punchline: The punchline is the word 'Jabroni' — a wrestling slang insult — delivered as the unanimous verdict of an entire room of wedding guests, which is inherently absurd.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the specific word 'Jabroni' and the unanimous-consensus framing. It's a quick background gag during the montage — not developed enough to be more than a minor laugh.

jokes.text: And then everyone said, 'Jabroni!' / Jabroni! This fucking guy, unbelievable! Hop in.
jokes.setup: During the peak of the wedding celebration montage
jokes.punchline: The inexplicable use of 'Jabroni' (a wrestling insult/slang) as a celebration exclamation, treated as the punch of a shared story
jokes.explanation: The randomness of 'Jabroni' in this context is funny but it's more a vibe beat than a crafted joke. Gets by on energy.

jokes.text: Sarah, I feel like I don't even know you. / It's Vivian.
jokes.setup: John and a woman have apparently just shared an intimate moment (implied by the montage/music).
jokes.punchline: John uses the wrong name — 'Sarah' — immediately after what should be a romantic moment. She corrects him flatly.
jokes.explanation: The setup 'I feel like I don't even know you' creates an expectation of romantic depth — the punchline is that he literally doesn't know her name. Classic comedic inversion. The irony is rich (he's right; he doesn't know her). The economy is excellent — two lines, a lot of comedic information.

jokes.text: Would you say you're completely full of shit or just 50%? / I hope just 50, but who knows?
jokes.setup: In what appears to be an intimate post-wedding moment, a woman directly confronts John about his authenticity.
jokes.punchline: John concedes the point but can't even be certain of his own percentage — the self-aware admission of incurable dishonesty.
jokes.explanation: The 'just 50, but who knows?' answer is a great character moment — honest about dishonesty, with a philosophical shrug that's both charming and self-aware. The uncertainty ('but who knows?') is the best part: he can't even commit to his own level of bullshit. Very character-specific for John.

jokes.text: You don't think we're being... I don't want to say sleazy, 'cause that's not the right word, but a little irresponsible, maybe? / No! / One day, you'll look back on all this and laugh, say we were young and stupid.
jokes.setup: After a long successful wedding-crashing season, John has a moment of conscience.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy instantly shuts down the moral concern with 'No!' then pivots to the 'young and stupid' frame — except the 'we're not that young' punchline is coming.
jokes.explanation: The setup for the 'we're not that young' punchline. Functional character-comedy beat — Jeremy's refusal to even consider the question is good characterization but the joke needs its payoff.

jokes.text: We're not that young.
jokes.setup: Jeremy insists they'll look back as 'young and stupid' kids. John has been going along with it.
jokes.punchline: John's quiet 'We're not that young' — a beat of genuine self-awareness that undercuts the nostalgia Jeremy was selling.
jokes.explanation: Four words. The entire comedic and thematic point of the scene is delivered in four words. 'We're not that young' works as a joke (the deflation of Jeremy's self-serving narrative) and as a character beat (John's creeping awareness of his arrested development). Perfect economy — 10/10. The pause before it and the matter-of-fact delivery make it land even harder. This is one of the best jokes in the reel: the craft is in what it DOESN'T say.

jokes.text: Oh! Baba ganoush. What do we got? Christmas come early.
jokes.setup: Jeremy spots something exciting — it turns out to be an article about the Cleary wedding.
jokes.punchline: His exclamation of 'Baba ganoush' as a general expression of delight (like a mild oath or celebratory outburst) is a funny specific word choice — a Middle Eastern dip as an expression of joy.
jokes.explanation: 'Baba ganoush' as an exclamation is a character-specific verbal tic that's funny because it's so random. 'Christmas come early' as a cliché is then set up for the wedding-season payoff. Light but charming.

jokes.text: This is the Kentucky Derby of weddings.
jokes.setup: John is reluctant to crash one more wedding at the end of the season.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's framing of a Cabinet Secretary's daughter's wedding as the Super Bowl/Kentucky Derby of their wedding-crashing 'sport' is a hyperbolic escalation that reveals how seriously they take their hobby.
jokes.explanation: The Kentucky Derby framing is a solid piece of sports-analogy comedy. It upgrades wedding crashing to a competitive athletic pursuit and frames the Clearys as a prestige target. Economical and character-revealing.

jokes.text: This is the Kentucky Derby of weddings. / Pal, there's gonna be over 200 single women at this wedding.
jokes.setup: John is hesitant about crashing the Secretary of the Treasury's daughter's wedding
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's sales pitch reduces the entire Secretary's legacy to: 200 single women and good finger food
jokes.explanation: 'Kentucky Derby of weddings' is a solid metaphor. The enumeration of three live bands, oysters, and finger food as Jeremy's key selling points is funny character work.

jokes.text: Oh, please don't take a turn to negative town.
jokes.setup: John complains that he's tired and his feet hurt — standard reluctance.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's rebuke is to personify negativity as a geographic destination — 'negative town' — with the casual delivery of someone who has coined a philosophy.
jokes.explanation: 'Negative town' is a nicely inventive piece of Vaughn-speak. The personification of emotional states as places is a recognizable comedy move but 'negative town' is specific enough to feel fresh. Very quotable.

jokes.text: At the Buckner nuptials you were sitting and sulking in the corner. / I wasn't sulking. I twisted my ankle.
jokes.setup: Jeremy is trying to motivate John, citing a past example of his poor performance.
jokes.punchline: John's defense — 'I twisted my ankle' — sounds like a child's excuse, suggesting either (a) he is lying and was indeed sulking or (b) this is genuinely how they think about wedding crashing.
jokes.explanation: Light character sparring. The ankle excuse is funny because it's exactly the kind of implausible defense that makes the sulking theory more credible. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: Rule #6: Do not sit in the corner and sulk. It draws attention to you in a negative way. Draw attention to yourself, but on your own terms.
jokes.setup: John denies sulking. Jeremy escalates to quoting the official 'rules.'
jokes.punchline: The existence of formalized, numbered wedding-crashing rules — with the specificity of 'draws attention to you in a negative way' — reveals an entire subculture the film has invented.
jokes.explanation: The 'Rules' device is a great comedic worldbuilding tool. The specificity of Rule #6 — the distinction between 'negative attention' and positive self-direction — is funny because it's real advice that's been formalized into wedding-crashing scripture.

jokes.text: When Chaz Reinhold passed the sacred rules of wedding crashing onto us 12 years ago, he gave us a legacy. / You make it sound like a cult, okay? And from everything you've told me about Chaz, he sounds like a kook!
jokes.setup: Jeremy elevates the rules to near-religious significance, invoking the mythic founder 'Chaz Reinhold.'
jokes.punchline: John cuts through the reverence: 'you make it sound like a cult' and dismisses the legend as 'a kook.'
jokes.explanation: The mythologizing of a wedding-crashing guru is an excellent absurdist comic premise. John's reality-check ('sounds like a cult / a kook') is the straight-man puncture that makes the whole structure work.

jokes.text: He is a brave and a decent man. He is a pioneer! / He lived with his mother till he was 40! She tried to poison his oatmeal! / Erroneous! Erroneous on both counts!
jokes.setup: Jeremy defends Chaz Reinhold's honor after John calls him a kook.
jokes.punchline: John reveals the specific biographical detail — 'lived with his mother till 40, she tried to poison his oatmeal' — to which Jeremy responds with the bizarrely formal 'Erroneous! Erroneous on both counts!'
jokes.explanation: Two great jokes in rapid succession. First: 'she tried to poison his oatmeal' — a specific, absurd biographical detail that demolishes the 'pioneer' framing while also raising more questions than it answers. Second: 'Erroneous! Erroneous on both counts!' — Jeremy's indignant legal-sounding rebuttal is a perfect non-answer that only deepens the comedy. 'Erroneous on both counts' as a formal denial of something absurd is extremely quotable. The escalation structure is tight.

jokes.text: Secret Service. Consequences.
jokes.setup: Jeremy is trying to persuade John to crash the high-profile Cleary wedding.
jokes.punchline: He lists the heightened stakes of crashing a Cabinet Secretary's wedding in two words, as if that settles the matter — 'Secret Service. Consequences.' The understatement of acknowledging and immediately dismissing serious risk.
jokes.explanation: Two-word joke with 10/10 economy. The rhythm of 'Secret Service. Consequences.' — said as brief acknowledgment rather than deterrent — is funny because Jeremy has named real risks and then set them aside by simply naming them. The pause implied between the two nouns is doing comedic work.

jokes.text: Sailing? / Sailing's like sex to these people. They love it.
jokes.setup: John questions why sailing terminology is in the dossier.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's 'sailing's like sex to these people' — delivered with total authority — reduces the upper-class obsession with sailing to a libidinal fixation.
jokes.explanation: 'Sailing's like sex to these people' is a confident, specific class-satire observation delivered with Vaughn's characteristic casual authority. The comparison makes immediate intuitive sense (and pays off in the vows later).

jokes.text: Let's be from Vermont and let's have an emerging maple syrup conglomerate. / Wait, that's stupid. We don't know anything about maple syrup. / I happen to know everything there is to know about maple syrup. I love maple syrup. I love maple syrup on pancakes. I love it on pizza. I like to take maple syrup and put a little bit in my hair when I've had a rough week. What do you think holds it up, slick?
jokes.setup: John and Jeremy debate their cover backstory. John dismisses the maple syrup idea because 'we don't know anything about it.'
jokes.punchline: Jeremy launches into an escalating catalog of maple syrup uses that starts plausibly (pancakes) and ends with using it as hair product — the punchline 'What do you think holds it up, slick?' retroactively making it autobiographical.
jokes.explanation: One of the best Vaughn riffs in the reel. The structure is perfectly engineered: pancakes → pizza (mild escalation) → hair product (full commitment to the absurd) → 'What do you think holds it up, slick?' (the kicker that makes it personal). The word 'slick' doing double duty as a hair-product pun AND an address is a lovely touch. 'I happen to know everything there is to know about maple syrup' as a preface to what follows is great setup. Character-specific: only Jeremy would have this relationship with maple syrup.

jokes.text: It's the first quarter of the big game and you want to toss up a Hail Mary! I'd like to be pimps from Oakland or cowboys from Arizona, but it's not Halloween! Grow up, Peter Pan! Count Chocula!
jokes.setup: John rejects the maple syrup backstory as too risky for the highest-stakes wedding they've ever attempted.
jokes.punchline: His rant escalates from sports metaphor to 'pimps from Oakland' to 'cowboys from Arizona' — suggesting these are actual backstories he's considered — and ends with the insults 'Peter Pan' and 'Count Chocula' in rapid succession.
jokes.explanation: 'Count Chocula' as a withering insult is genuinely funny — it's specific, unexpected, and reveals John's creative insult vocabulary. 'Pimps from Oakland or cowboys from Arizona' implies a whole rejected-backstory catalogue that is funnier for not being explained. The 'it's not Halloween' pivot is the structural key: it demotes the fantasy personas from possible to impossible.

jokes.text: No, don't waste your time on girls with hats, they tend to be very proper. / Yeah? The proper girl in the hat just eye-fucked the shit outta me.
jokes.setup: John spots an attractive woman in a hat and is immediately cautioned by Jeremy: hat girls are 'very proper.'
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's generalization is instantly demolished — the woman has eye-fucked Jeremy with enormous aggression.
jokes.explanation: 'Eye-fucked the shit outta me' is a memorably crude phrasing for a very specific social interaction, delivered with casual matter-of-factness that makes it funnier. The structure is tight: rule stated, rule immediately disproven. The specificity of 'the shit outta me' — suggesting extraordinary intensity — escalates the crudeness to the right comedic pitch. Very quotable.

jokes.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. / Why don't you say it a little louder? I don't think the priest heard you.
jokes.setup: Jeremy apparently said 'eye-fucked the shit outta me' aloud during a wedding ceremony.
jokes.punchline: John's mock-apologetic 'Why don't you say it a little louder' implies Jeremy's vulgarity has already compromised their cover in a sacred setting.
jokes.explanation: A classic 'too loud in a quiet place' comedy beat. The image of this phrase echoing in a wedding ceremony is funny. Functional but not exceptional — the joke type is well-worn.

jokes.text: Look, John, I'm sorry I'm not sorry, okay? I'm not gonna apologize. I'm a cocksman.
jokes.setup: John criticizes Jeremy for the loudness of his vulgarity during the ceremony.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm a cocksman' — delivered as a simple statement of identity, as though it's a recognized profession or life philosophy that excuses all behavior.
jokes.explanation: 'I'm a cocksman' is an extraordinary three-word character declaration. The unapologetic self-labeling, the archaism of the word 'cocksman,' and the gravity with which it's delivered combine into one of the film's signature lines. It functions as a philosophy-of-life statement with maximum economy. The setup 'I'm sorry I'm not sorry' is decent, but 'I'm a cocksman' as the closing justification is what makes this exceptional. Very high character integration — this could only be Jeremy.

jokes.text: Tourette's.
jokes.setup: Frank Myers nearby has apparently heard Jeremy's outburst. John needs to explain it instantly.
jokes.punchline: John's one-word explanation — 'Tourette's' — is a breezy, socially inappropriate lie that covers the situation with maximum economy.
jokes.explanation: One-word joke with perfect economy. The Tourette's excuse is not entirely original (it's been used before) but deployed here with the right speed and confidence. Scores lower on originality because it's a known comedy move, but the execution is tight.

jokes.text: We are Uncle Ned's kids. / Uncle Ned. / Is he Liz's brother? / Uncle Ned, the brother of Aunt Liz. / How is everybody? / Well, Dad kinda putters around the house. Hey, Aunt Liz sends her best. She couldn't make it. / Yeah, I know. Uh... she's dead. From the grave. She sends her best from the grave.
jokes.setup: John and Jeremy improvise a cover story, claiming to be 'Uncle Ned's kids.' Jeremy invents that Aunt Liz 'couldn't make it.'
jokes.punchline: Frank informs them that Aunt Liz is dead — John has to scramble, landing on the increasingly absurd 'From the grave. She sends her best from the grave.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent cringe escalation. The punchline is built in two steps: (1) she's dead — moderate cringe, and (2) John's recovery 'She sends her best from the grave' — the best version of the worst thing to say. 'From the grave' repeated for emphasis as though that clarifies things is the comedic peak. The structure rewards the buildup: each line digs deeper. High rewatch bonus because on rewatch you can see Jeremy's face fall when 'she's dead' is announced.

jokes.text: she's dead. / From the grave. / She sends her best from the grave.
jokes.setup: John and Jeremy are enthusiastically talking about Aunt Liz — who the guest then reveals is dead
jokes.punchline: John's recovery — 'From the grave' and 'She sends her best from the grave' — doubles down rather than retreating, turning it into an increasingly surreal commitment to the lie
jokes.explanation: Very well-structured cringe-comedy. The correct move is to apologize; instead they escalate into the supernatural. 'She sends her best from the grave' is a great dark comedy line — specific, committed, and completely inappropriate. The 'We've become extremely spiritual' topper makes it even better.

jokes.text: We've become extremely spiritual ever since she passed. / Thank you so much for your kindness, brother. Lord knows we need family now more than ever.
jokes.setup: Frank has just been told that Aunt Liz is sending her best 'from the grave.'
jokes.punchline: John and Jeremy pivot immediately to solemn grief performance — 'Lord knows we need family now more than ever' — extracting maximum sympathy from the fictional dead aunt.
jokes.explanation: A good escalation of the Aunt Liz joke. The speed with which they weaponize the fictional dead aunt is funny, and 'Lord knows we need family now more than ever' is absurdly over-the-top religious solemnity that sells the con.

jokes.text: How many times are you gonna do this shit? / Rule #32: You don't commit to a relative unless you're absolutely positive that they have a pulse. / Rule 16: Give me an up-to-date family tree. That was your mistake. / Rule #76: No excuses, play like a champion.
jokes.setup: John is furious at Jeremy for committing to 'Aunt Liz' without knowing she was dead.
jokes.punchline: Both men immediately retreat to quoting the Rules of Wedding Crashing at each other — including Rule #76 'No excuses, play like a champion' — which is actually solid practical advice for any competitive pursuit.
jokes.explanation: The Rules device pays off beautifully here. Rule #32 ('positive they have a pulse') is a perfect absurd rule — specific to exactly the scenario that just happened. 'No excuses, play like a champion' (Rule #76) is the strongest of the three: it's genuinely motivational and completely inappropriate to the context. High quotability across all three rules.

jokes.text: Hello, Red. / Dibs. / She's all yours. / I ain't gonna fight you.
jokes.setup: During the Cleary wedding ceremony, one of the men spots an attractive woman.
jokes.punchline: The 'dibs' call and 'I ain't gonna fight you' response reduces romantic interest to schoolyard territory-claiming — delivered with total seriousness.
jokes.explanation: The 'dibs' joke is not original but its deployment here — during a wedding ceremony, in complete earnest — works because of the character context. 'I ain't gonna fight you' implies a code of honor among the crashers that is funnier than the dibs itself.

jokes.text: I think we've got a crier. / No shot. / $20. / Make it 40. / Done. [Woman begins crying]
jokes.setup: John and Jeremy spot a woman in the congregation who may be about to cry during the ceremony.
jokes.punchline: They immediately start betting on it — treating a romantic ceremony as a sporting event with over/under odds.
jokes.explanation: The betting structure is tight and economical — five lines, complete comedic transaction. The punchline is the confirmation (she cries), and the rapid escalation from $20 to $40 reveals both men's instant competitive investment. The character-specific element is that they're doing this DURING a ceremony — their irreverence is perfectly calibrated.

jokes.text: $20, 1 Corinthians. / Double or nothing, Colossians 3:12.
jokes.setup: Following the crying bet, the men continue gambling — this time on which Bible passage the bride's sister will read.
jokes.punchline: They are betting on specific scripture citations during a wedding ceremony, with the implied expertise of people who have heard a LOT of these readings.
jokes.explanation: A great escalation of the betting gag. Betting on scripture citations requires that you've attended hundreds of weddings — the specificity of 'Colossians 3:12' versus '1 Corinthians' (the obvious Love Is Patient choice) is funny because it shows genuine connoisseurship. The fact that the common choice (1 Corinthians) wins is itself a payoff: they've been crashing so many weddings that the data says the obvious pick wins.

jokes.text: "Love is patient, love is kind." [Corinthians winner confirmed]
jokes.setup: Jeremy bet on 1 Corinthians (the 'love is patient' reading); John bet on Colossians.
jokes.punchline: Gloria reads 1 Corinthians — the obvious, clichéd wedding reading — confirming Jeremy's bet, implying John lost his money on the exotic Colossians pick.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the scripture bet. Its comedy is entirely dependent on the setup — as a standalone moment it's nothing, but as a resolution to the bet it lands. The humor is in knowing John lost money on Colossians.

jokes.text: As you all know, Craig and Christina are quite the sailing enthusiasts. In that light, they have elected to exchange vows which they themselves have written.
jokes.setup: Jeremy told John 'sailing is like sex to these people' during their preparation
jokes.punchline: Sure enough, the vows are entirely in sailing metaphors — the callback to Jeremy's briefing pays off, confirming his anthropological insight was correct
jokes.explanation: Good structural payoff. The fact that the entire vow ceremony is in sailing terminology validates Jeremy's prep work and sets up the punchline of 'first mate.'

jokes.text: I, Craig, take you, Christina, to be my wife, my best friend and my first mate... through sickness and health, clear skies and squalls. / I'm sorry, I have a tickle in my throat.
jokes.setup: Craig and Christina exchange sailing-themed wedding vows — paying off the 'sailing is like sex to these people' joke from earlier.
jokes.punchline: Craig's vows include 'clear skies and squalls' and 'first mate' — the sailing metaphor taken to absurdist extremes — before he is interrupted by what sounds like tears or emotion, awkwardly covered as 'a tickle in my throat.'
jokes.explanation: A satisfying payoff to the sailing worldbuilding. 'First mate' and 'clear skies and squalls' are exactly the kind of nautical vow insertions that are funny because they're simultaneously sincere and ridiculous. The 'tickle in my throat' beat is the right understated topper.

jokes.text: I, Christina, take you, Craig, to be my best friend, and my captain... to be your anchor and your sail... your starboard and your port. / Well, this is a first.
jokes.setup: Craig's already-absurd sailing vows have set a high bar. Christina now delivers hers.
jokes.punchline: Christina goes even further — 'anchor and your sail, your starboard and your port' — covering the full nautical vocabulary. One of the men's reaction: 'Well, this is a first.'
jokes.explanation: The escalation of nautical vow density — now including starboard AND port — is good escalation comedy. The 'Well, this is a first' reaction is a perfect deadpan understatement that lands as the kicker for the entire sailing-vows bit. Even seasoned wedding crashers who've heard everything haven't heard this.

jokes.text: You may kiss the first mate.
jokes.setup: The wedding officiant has sat through the entire sailing-themed ceremony.
jokes.punchline: Instead of the traditional 'you may kiss the bride,' the officiant has gone full nautical: 'you may kiss the first mate.'
jokes.explanation: The perfect button on the sailing joke arc. 'You may kiss the first mate' is six words that deliver the full comedic payoff of three separate setup jokes. The officiant committing to the nautical terminology rather than using the standard phrase is what makes this land — it shows the entire culture has been infected by the sailing obsession. Near-perfect economy and structure. This is what a well-earned callback looks like.

jokes.text: John sarcastically agrees the wedding is 'first class all the way' while eating hors d'oeuvres off a sampler tray
jokes.setup: Jeremy promised the wedding would be 'classy'
jokes.punchline: John repeats 'class class class' in a hollow, deadpan tone while stuffing his face, confirming it is indeed classy — or just that he doesn't care
jokes.explanation: Light opening gag — the repetition of 'class class class' is a soft ironic beat, functional but not particularly crafted. Sets tone without landing hard.

jokes.text: Jeremy's parting instructions: 'I'm going to go drop this box of fresh Wyoming air. If you see any crab cakes, get your hands on some — 'cause I love the crab cakes.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy is giving John logistical crash-the-wedding instructions
jokes.punchline: He interrupts tactical wedding-crashing strategy with an urgent, sincere request for crab cakes, treating them with the same gravity as the mission
jokes.explanation: The 'fresh Wyoming air' euphemism for the gift scam is funny on its own, but the pivot to sincere crab-cake obsession is the real joke. It's character-specific to Jeremy's chaotic id — his appetites always upstage his schemes. Good economy and character integration.

jokes.text: John identifies every wrapped gift by its contents — fondue set, knife set, massage oils — without opening them
jokes.setup: Claire is holding a gift and John claims to be psychic
jokes.punchline: He rattles off every gift accurately, including 'massage oils and a book on tantra from the wacky aunt,' revealing that this is a well-practiced wedding-crashing intelligence skill, not psychic ability
jokes.explanation: The escalating gift-identification sequence is well-structured: each correct answer raises the stakes, culminating in the tantra book being the peak reveal. The 'wacky aunt' specification adds texture. Good structure and character integration — this is a flirting tactic that shows John's specific brand of charming con-artistry.

jokes.text: 'Massage oils and a book on tantra from the wacky aunt' — confirmed by 'Aunt Millie'
jokes.setup: John predicted the gift was tantra oils from 'the wacky aunt'
jokes.punchline: Claire checks the tag — it's from 'Aunt Millie,' confirming John's spot-on read of wedding-guest archetypes
jokes.explanation: The payoff confirmation beat is crisp and earns a bigger laugh than the initial prediction because structure is everything here — the two-beat delivery (predict, confirm) is classic comedy architecture executed cleanly.

jokes.text: 'Unfortunately my powers only apply to useless consumer products. Well, if the police are missing a Belgian waffle maker, you could give 'em a hand.'
jokes.setup: John has just demonstrated 'psychic' gift-reading ability
jokes.punchline: Claire's quip about helping police find a Belgian waffle maker deflates the mystique perfectly, and John's self-deprecating setup ('useless consumer products') invites the punchline Claire delivers
jokes.explanation: Claire's comeback is sharp and specific — 'Belgian waffle maker' is funnier than any generic appliance, and the police procedural frame is a good absurdist twist. Establishes Claire as a worthy sparring partner. Good economy and wit.

jokes.text: Jeremy spots a woman and says 'Isn't that the girl you hooked up with at the Andersons' wedding?'
jokes.setup: The wedding-crashing world these men inhabit involves serial hook-ups at weddings across the social circuit
jokes.punchline: The casualness of 'the Andersons' wedding' implies a vast personal database of previous conquests organized by wedding name — played completely straight
jokes.explanation: Functional plot-comedy beat. The humor is in the implied lifestyle, not the line itself. Sets up the 'Shlomo' sequence which is the real payoff.

jokes.text: Jeremy pretends John is 'Shlomo,' who renounced his possessions to move to Nepal — until a scuba diving accident left him deaf, amnesiac, and unrecognizable even to his 'own brother'
jokes.setup: John is about to be recognized by a previous hook-up, requiring an escape from the playbook
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's cover story accumulates absurd detail upon absurd detail — Nepal renunciation, scuba accident, oxygen deprivation amnesia, and total deafness — each layer more outrageous than the last
jokes.explanation: This is Vince Vaughn in full motor-mouth improv mode — the escalating absurdity is precisely calibrated. Each new detail (Nepal, scuba, deafness, 'even me, his own brother') is funnier than the last. The structure is an escalating con that keeps topping itself. High character integration: only Jeremy would improvise this particular flavor of insane cover story with this much conviction.

jokes.text: 'He actually can't hear anything either. It's part of the accident.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy has already sold the scuba accident/amnesia story and the woman is sympathizing
jokes.punchline: Jeremy adds deafness as a casual afterthought — 'part of the accident' — delivered with complete earnestness, piling on one more absurd detail
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — five words to add a whole new dimension to the lie. The deadpan delivery of 'part of the accident' as though it's a medical footnote is the essence of Vaughn's comedic style here. Great economy score.

jokes.text: Jeremy negotiates taking John/Shlomo to the bathroom AFTER getting him crab cakes — circling back to the crab-cake obsession
jokes.setup: Jeremy is trying to exit the conversation; John (as Shlomo) needs to be led away
jokes.punchline: Even in the middle of a high-stakes con escape, Jeremy prioritizes the crab cakes over the bathroom, treating a deaf amnesiac's snack before his bodily needs
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback — the crab cake fixation returns at the worst possible moment, showing Jeremy's id overriding even self-preservation. The character consistency is the joke.

jokes.text: 'Everyone wants to be a part of a miracle. I turned a corner. She's a part of it. People helping people. It's powerful stuff.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy asks how John plans to call the woman given she thinks he's deaf
jokes.punchline: John's completely straight-faced plan to spin his fake recovery as a miracle she was part of — delivered with the sincerity of a motivational speaker
jokes.explanation: Owen Wilson's gift is delivering sociopathic logic with warm sincerity. 'People helping people. It's powerful stuff.' is a great button — the faux-inspirational tone applied to a shameless con. Good character integration.

jokes.text: John announces his angle: balloon animals for kids, then 'when she comes close, guess who's a broken man — haunted past'
jokes.setup: The two are strategizing their separate seduction approaches
jokes.punchline: John's plan involves using children as props and then pivoting to performed emotional damage — 'haunted past' delivered as a tactical menu item
jokes.explanation: The clinical vocabulary of seduction tactics ('haunted past') is funny precisely because it's itemized so matter-of-factly. Good character work showing John's systematic predation dressed up as charm.

jokes.text: 'Uncle Jeremy's a little tired right now, so why don't we do something like... a giraffe?'
jokes.setup: A child demands a bicycle made of balloons; Jeremy is in the middle of a seduction strategy
jokes.punchline: Jeremy negotiates down from a bicycle to a giraffe with the exhausted, patronizing tone of a man who is completely over children
jokes.explanation: The 'Uncle Jeremy' self-reference is a nice touch — he's so deep in character he's adopting the uncle role. The exhausted negotiation with a child is relatable comedy ground, executed with Vaughn energy.

jokes.text: Child screams 'I just want a bicycle!' and when Jeremy asks why he's yelling, the kid says 'Whatever, make me a bicycle, clown!'
jokes.setup: Jeremy tries to manage a demanding child while using balloon animals as a seduction prop
jokes.punchline: 'Make me a bicycle, clown!' — a child speaking to an adult with the entitlement and contempt of a mob boss is the comedic inversion. 'Whatever' makes it perfect.
jokes.explanation: 'Make me a bicycle, clown!' has become one of the most quoted lines from this film. The comedic inversion — a small child with the aggressive authority of an insulting customer — delivered with 'Whatever' as a dismissive setup is sharp. The economy is perfect: four words do all the work. High quotability score justified by its cultural afterlife.

jokes.text: Jeremy stares at the bicycle balloon he's making, muttering 'I'm gonna make you a bicycle. But I don't want to make you a bicycle.' Then the child: 'Shut your mouth, funny guy, and make it!'
jokes.setup: Jeremy has been commanded to make the bicycle; he complies but voices impotent resistance
jokes.punchline: His quiet internal monologue rebellion is immediately silenced by the child's 'Shut your mouth, funny guy' — the child has total dominance, Jeremy has none
jokes.explanation: The continuation escalates beautifully — Jeremy's pathetic sotto voce resistance ('I don't want to make you a bicycle') is instantly crushed by 'Shut your mouth, funny guy.' The power dynamic inversion is fully committed and extremely specific to Vince Vaughn's energy. The child is now a full comedic antagonist.

jokes.text: Jeremy dismisses the child with 'Let's see how you do with somebody your own age' and immediately flirts with an older woman
jokes.setup: Jeremy has just been dominated by a child and needs an ego escape
jokes.punchline: 'Let's see how you do with somebody your own age' is meant to rebuke the child but doubles as Jeremy re-entering adult seduction mode — the segue is instant and shameless
jokes.explanation: Good transitional joke. The double meaning (challenging the child / pivoting to adult flirting) is efficiently handled. Jeremy's resilience/shamelessness is the character note.

jokes.text: Jeremy claims he built 'an exact replica, to scale, of Wrigley Field' out of balloons last week — 'I don't have anywhere to put it.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy is boasting about his balloon skills to the older woman
jokes.punchline: The specificity of Wrigley Field (not just 'a stadium') and the practical problem of storage ('I don't have anywhere to put it') elevate this from generic boasting to absurdist specificity
jokes.explanation: The 'I don't have anywhere to put it' is the key line — taking the absurd premise seriously with a practical logistics problem. Good economy. The woman's response ('Okay, then I'll take a sportscar') matching his energy makes it land harder.

jokes.text: John asks Secretary Cleary's wife how long they've been married; she says '30 years next April.' Then: 'Yeah, and we were faithful for two of them.'
jokes.setup: John is making polite conversation about their long marriage, expecting a sweet answer
jokes.punchline: 'We were faithful for two of them' — delivered completely casually, as though this is a normal and acceptable marriage statistic, then 'Enjoy the party' as an instant subject-closer
jokes.explanation: One of the sharpest one-liners in this reel. Perfect economy — the setup is a totally straight romantic question, the punchline is delivered as banal fact, and 'Enjoy the party' closes it with a dismissive button that refuses to let John process what he just heard. The dark subversion of the 30-year marriage ideal in nine words is excellent craft.

jokes.text: John claims to have read Secretary Cleary's obscure position paper on 'economic expansion in Micronesia' while sailing his boat to Bermuda
jokes.setup: John is cold-approaching the powerful Secretary of the Treasury at his daughter's wedding
jokes.punchline: The specificity of the paper topic (Micronesia), combined with the nonchalant detail of reading it 'while sailing to Bermuda,' creates a portrait of John as an implausibly well-prepared social con man
jokes.explanation: The humor is in John's shameless performance — the obscure paper title and the casual lifestyle detail ('sailing to Bermuda') are both choices that reveal his gift for targeted flattery. Competent but not a standout moment.

jokes.text: John enthusiastically agrees to smoke 'stogies' on the deck with the Secretary of the Treasury, then immediately looks pained
jokes.setup: John has successfully charmed Secretary Cleary into a private cigar session — a seduction victory
jokes.punchline: The implied visual: John has talked himself into a situation he can't escape, forced to smoke cigars with a powerful politician he's deceiving. His enthusiasm ('Stogies?') followed by the trapped reality is the beat.
jokes.explanation: Light transitional beat — the 'Stogies?' with its overenthusiastic acceptance is a small character laugh, but the visual payoff (John stuck on the deck) carries more weight than the dialogue alone.

jokes.text: 'It's just that we lost a lot of really good men out there.' — Jeremy's inexplicable non-sequitur to the older woman
jokes.setup: Jeremy has been dancing with the older woman; she's told him they need to go
jokes.punchline: Jeremy suddenly drops a war-memorial gravitas line completely out of context — 'we lost a lot of really good men out there' — as if he's solemnly commemorating the dance floor
jokes.explanation: One of the most random and therefore delightful beats in the reel. Vaughn's delivery of this line — solemn, weighted, sincere — applied to a wedding dance floor is pure absurdist comedy. No setup, no payoff needed; the incongruity IS the joke. Specific enough to be memorable.

jokes.text: 'Thank you so much for the dance and it was wonderful to meet you. I wish I were stronger.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy is saying goodbye to the older woman after their dance
jokes.punchline: 'I wish I were stronger' — an inexplicable, melodramatic exit line implying he is being torn away against his will by forces beyond his control, applied to a casual wedding farewell
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the dance sequence. 'I wish I were stronger' implies a romantic torment that is completely manufactured and utterly unwarranted, but Vaughn delivers it with devastated sincerity. Extremely economical absurdism.

jokes.text: Secretary Cleary describes his son Todd: 'All I've seen him do is dribble his own blood on a canvas and smear it around with a stick!'
jokes.setup: Secretary Cleary is bemoaning his son's lack of direction and belief in 'art'
jokes.punchline: The father's reduction of blood-painting to its most clinical, contemptuous description — 'dribble his own blood... smear it around with a stick' — captures the total incomprehension of a pragmatist confronting avant-garde art
jokes.explanation: Strong character comedy — this line perfectly encapsulates a powerful, results-oriented man's baffled contempt for his artistic son. The precision of 'his own blood' and 'with a stick' as opposed to, say, brushes, reveals both the son's extremity and the father's refusal to even use the word 'painting.' High character integration.

jokes.text: John diplomatically suggests Todd is 'just trying to find his own way, his own path — you cast a pretty big shadow.' Secretary Cleary pauses, then: 'Death, you are my bitch lover!'
jokes.setup: John has gently mediated the father-son conversation; Todd has been brooding on the dock
jokes.punchline: Todd screams 'Death, you are my bitch lover!' at the ocean — a gothic melodrama outburst that arrives immediately after John's sincere diplomatic effort, undercutting it completely
jokes.explanation: One of the best comedic moments in this reel. The structure is impeccable: John's earnest 'you cast a pretty big shadow' sets up a sincere beat, then Todd's 'Death, you are my bitch lover!' demolishes it. The line itself is an almost perfect absurdist construction — specific ('bitch lover' rather than just 'lover'), addressed to an abstract concept, shouted at the ocean. Highly quotable, great character work establishing Todd as a comedic foil. John's response 'Todd, that's good! Tell that mean ocean!' is a perfect button. This approaches the 8+ threshold and justifies it on originality, structure, and character integration.

jokes.text: John, to Secretary Cleary, after Todd's outburst: 'Todd, that's good! Tell that mean ocean! Oh, uh... it's a start.'
jokes.setup: Todd has just screamed 'Death, you are my bitch lover!' at the ocean; John is standing next to the Secretary
jokes.punchline: John's instinctive encouragement ('Todd, that's good!') immediately gives way to the deflating 'it's a start' — he's desperately managing the Secretary's impression while acknowledging Todd's behavior is not quite there yet
jokes.explanation: The button on the Todd outburst. 'Tell that mean ocean' is absurdly supportive, and 'It's a start' is the perfect deadpan retreat. Owen Wilson's warm-but-floundering social management is a great character note. Good economy.

jokes.text: John's seduction speech to Gloria invoking Schopenhauer's 'metaphysical awareness' — that we are all one — culminates in a list: 'the Prime Minister of England, my cousin Harry, you and me, the fat kid from What's Happening!!, the Olsen twins, Natalie Portman, the guy who wrote Catcher in the Rye, Nat King Cole, Carrot Top, Jay-Z, Weird Al Yankovic, Harry Potter — if he existed — the whore on the street corner, your mother...'
jokes.setup: John is delivering a philosophical seduction monologue to Gloria, claiming oneness with all humanity via Schopenhauer
jokes.punchline: The list begins plausibly (Prime Minister, cousin Harry) and devolves into increasingly incongruous pop-culture figures, with the deliberate hedge 'if he existed' for Harry Potter, and 'your mother' as the final escalation that tips into the physical
jokes.explanation: The escalating list is a well-executed comedic structure — the pivot from philosophical to 'the fat kid from What's Happening!!' is perfectly chosen as the first gear-shift, and 'Carrot Top' and 'Weird Al Yankovic' are inspired mid-tier absurd choices. 'Harry Potter — if he existed' is a sharp specificity beat. 'Your mother' as the transition to physical contact is both a great closer and a classic misdirection. The Schopenhauer framing gives it intellectual structure that makes the absurdist content land harder.

jokes.text: 'Well, the guy wants to run for President.' / 'He thinks Moby Dick is a venereal disease.'
jokes.setup: Claire and Sack are discussing Secretary Cleary's political ambitions
jokes.punchline: Sack's 'He thinks Moby Dick is a venereal disease' — a perfect anti-intellectual burn that is specific, visual, and deeply unflattering for a presidential candidate
jokes.explanation: One of the sharpest one-liners in the reel. 'Moby Dick is a venereal disease' is simultaneously a critique of a character's ignorance, a good venereal disease joke, and a sly political satire, all in seven words. Near-perfect economy. High quotability.

jokes.text: Claire says the wedding guests are all 'suckling at the power teat'
jokes.setup: Claire is cynically dismissing the wedding guests as social climbers around her powerful father
jokes.punchline: 'Suckling at the power teat' — an unusually earthy metaphor for a politician's daughter, combining nursing-animal imagery with political power in a vivid, slightly gross compound
jokes.explanation: A memorable phrase — the vulgarity of 'teat' in Claire's sophisticated-daughter context is the joke. Good economy but less constructed as a joke, more of a vivid character detail.

jokes.text: 'True love is your soul's recognition of its counterpoint in another.' / 'Well, it's a little cheesy, but... I like it.' / 'I saw it on a bumper sticker.'
jokes.setup: Claire asks what true love is; John delivers a beautiful, sincere-sounding definition that lands emotionally
jokes.punchline: 'I saw it on a bumper sticker' — instantly deflates the romantic sincerity, revealing John's philosophical depth was entirely outsourced, while somehow making him MORE charming
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in this reel and one of the film's signature moments. The structure is a textbook misdirection: a genuinely moving romantic declaration followed by an instant, complete deflation. The twist reveals John's character — a con man who accidentally stumbles into real connection while admitting he's reading from a bumper sticker. The fact that it somehow works on Claire, and the audience, makes it land on two levels simultaneously. The economy is exceptional — four words undoes and re-does everything the previous sentence built.

jokes.text: John advises Claire that the 'funny-because-it's-true bit only works if the truth is a small thing like everyone knows Jennifer likes to shop'
jokes.setup: Claire is planning a toast that makes fun of her sister for caring about what people think
jokes.punchline: John's comedy-theory breakdown of when 'funny because it's true' works is itself a meta joke — a wedding-crasher doing stand-up comedy craft analysis at a reception
jokes.explanation: A smart meta beat — John is essentially giving comedy-writing notes to Claire. Competent and character-revealing but not a standout joke on its own.

jokes.text: John predicts Claire will 'hear crickets' and 'sounds of silence'; Claire bets on the toast; John says 'Go walk the plank' / 'Hey, meet me at the back of the room — I'll be the guy waiting to say I told you so.'
jokes.setup: John has predicted Claire's toast will bomb; she's going to give it anyway
jokes.punchline: The playful antagonism of 'go walk the plank' + 'I'll be the guy waiting to say I told you so' establishes the comedic double-bet: will the toast bomb as foreshadowed?
jokes.explanation: Setup joke for the toast sequence — the humor is in the structured dramatic irony (we're told the toast will fail before it happens). 'Go walk the plank' has nice swagger. Functional storytelling comedy.

jokes.text: The first toast — a man at the podium reveals '...and so after my ninth stint in rehab, Craig was the only one who still believed in me. Been sober now for eight months. I love you, man.'
jokes.setup: The toast speeches are beginning; we expect wedding-convention sentiment
jokes.punchline: 'Ninth stint in rehab' — a classic escalation of a confessional toast that derails into genuine emotional need. 'I love you, man' to the groom from someone who is essentially not a friend of the couple but a rehabilitation case study.
jokes.explanation: 'Ninth stint' is the specificity that sells the joke — not 'multiple' but specifically nine. The escalation from normal wedding toast to addiction recovery testimony is well-paced, and 'I love you, man' landing as a sincere but socially awkward button is good dark comedy.

jokes.text: Claire gives her toast: 'I never thought my sister would find someone who cared about what other people thought as much as she did — until I met Craig.' Then awkward silence.
jokes.setup: John predicted this toast would bomb; Claire delivers the 'funny because it's true' line John explicitly warned her against
jokes.punchline: The room goes silent — the comedic payoff of the earlier setup. The double-edged toast reads as an insult in the room, confirming John's comedy-theory note exactly
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured payoff — the toast bomb delivers on three levels simultaneously: (1) John's prediction comes true, (2) it validates his comedy-craft analysis, (3) Claire's discomfort is a cringe beat with real emotional stakes. The structure score is high because this is the payoff of a carefully laid sequence. The silence itself is the punchline.

jokes.text: Claire tries to recover her toast: '...they both like the color green, like Craig's eyes and money.'
jokes.setup: Claire is floundering after her bomb toast; she pivots to find something in common between the couple
jokes.punchline: 'Like Craig's eyes and money' — an accidental second insult that implies Craig is mercenary, digging the hole deeper
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the failing toast is well-executed — 'Craig's eyes and money' is exactly the kind of recovery attempt that makes things worse. The structure of piling disaster on disaster in a toast context is reliable cringe comedy, and the specific word 'money' paired with 'eyes' is a sharp absurd image.

jokes.text: Claire abandons her prepared toast and delivers John's 'bumper sticker' true love line: 'Someone once told me that true love is the soul's recognition of its counterpoint in another.'
jokes.setup: Claire's toast has completely bombed; she pivots to something from the heart
jokes.punchline: She uses John's bumper-sticker line — the one he admitted was not his — as the genuine, moving core of her rescue toast, and it works perfectly
jokes.explanation: A satisfying structural callback — the bumper-sticker line John admitted was stolen is now Claire's sincere salvation. The irony that a con man's recycled wisdom becomes a moment of genuine feeling lands emotionally and comedically. High structure and character integration scores because this callback does real thematic work, not just comedy work.

jokes.text: 'I always knew my first time would be on a beach.'
jokes.setup: Gloria and Jeremy have just come up from below deck after an extended time below; Gloria is glowing
jokes.punchline: The line retroactively reveals they had sex — and that Gloria was a virgin — delivered with dreamy romantic satisfaction as though it's the fulfillment of a lifelong dream
jokes.explanation: A delayed reveal done cleanly — 'first time on a beach' works as misdirection (maybe she means something innocent) until Jeremy's reaction confirms the worst. The comedy is in Jeremy's dawning horror rather than the line itself.

jokes.text: Jeremy's reaction: face drains of color, shocked silence as Gloria says 'You were a virgin?'
jokes.setup: Gloria has just revealed it was her 'first time'
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's physical reaction — the implied visual of a man realizing he has accidentally taken someone's virginity at a wedding he crashed — is the punchline. 'Wow.' is all he manages.
jokes.explanation: Vaughn's physical reaction is the comedy — the dialogue is minimal ('Wow.') but the implied visual of his face is the laugh. Good character integration because Jeremy's horror is specific to his self-serving playbook being catastrophically broken.

jokes.text: 'Jeremy, we're gonna be so happy together. I love you!'
jokes.setup: Jeremy has just processed that Gloria was a virgin; she's now escalating to declarations of love and future life plans
jokes.punchline: Gloria's instant full-commitment declaration of love cements Jeremy's nightmare — a Stage Five situation he could not have predicted or prevented
jokes.explanation: The escalating horror of Gloria's sincerity is the joke — each revelation (virgin, love declaration, future plans) tightens the trap. Vaughn's silence/reaction carries most of the comedy here.

jokes.text: John introduces Claire to his 'boyfriend Sack' — John's reaction on meeting the large, aggressive Sack
jokes.setup: John has been charming Claire all wedding; she's told him he 'saved' her
jokes.punchline: Claire's boyfriend turns out to be a physically intimidating jock named 'Sack' who immediately redirects Claire with authority — John's face registers the abrupt obstacle
jokes.explanation: Plot comedy — the boyfriend reveal is a classic obstacle introduction. The name 'Sack' does comedy work on its own as a vaguely threatening monosyllable. 'Boom, I gotcha!' from Sack is a great alpha-male button.

jokes.text: John introduces Jeremy to Claire... who then introduces her boyfriend Sack. 'Uh, John, this is my boyfriend, Sack.'
jokes.setup: John and Claire have just shared an intimate moment. Claire is visibly moved and grateful.
jokes.punchline: The boyfriend reveal lands as a gut-punch — especially with the name 'Sack,' which is an absurd and slightly vulgar choice.
jokes.explanation: The reveal of a boyfriend is a classic rom-com gut-punch, and the name 'Sack' adds absurdist comedy to the sting. 'Hey fella' from Sack — dismissive and bro-ish — perfectly establishes him as an antagonist in one beat.

jokes.text: 'Boom, I gotcha!'
jokes.setup: Sack has just met John and immediately redirected Claire away
jokes.punchline: 'Boom, I gotcha!' — Sack celebrates catching his girlfriend talking to another man with the energy of someone who just won a competition, revealing an alpha-male insecurity and territorial aggression played as casual triumph
jokes.explanation: Two words that completely define a character type — the territorial alpha who treats social situations as competitions he wins. 'Boom, I gotcha!' is an instantly-readable villain/antagonist introduction disguised as casual cheer. Perfect economy and high character integration.

jokes.text: Jeremy to John: 'I've got a Stage Five clinger. No no, I need more time. Did you hear what I just said to you? Stage 5? Virgin? Clinger? Let's go, I'm gonna start the car.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy is trying to exit the wedding; John wants more time with Claire
jokes.punchline: The 'Stage Five clinger' taxonomy — delivered at increasing urgency and with the escalating list 'Stage 5? Virgin? Clinger?' — is a comedic inventory of Jeremy's specific nightmare situation
jokes.explanation: 'Stage Five clinger' has entered the pop-culture vocabulary as a phrase, which is the highest quotability test.
