The escalating list delivery is classic Vaughn — the rhythm of 'Stage 5? Virgin? Clinger?' is a comedic triple with panic built in. High character integration because this reveals the crashers' systematic taxonomy for women they exploit.

jokes.text: Jeremy: 'I'm terrified of this broad.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy has described Gloria as a Stage Five Virgin Clinger
jokes.punchline: 'I'm terrified of this broad' — the frank admission of fear from a man who professionally manipulates women is the comedic inversion. 'Broad' is a deliberately old-fashioned word that undercuts any self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: Good economy — 'terrified of this broad' in Vaughn's delivery is a perfect admission of impotence from someone who is never supposed to feel this way. 'Broad' as a word choice adds a retro-sleazy texture.

jokes.text: Jeremy's paranoid riff: 'He's the Secretary of the Treasury. And to be honest with you, my taxes aren't exactly in line. / He's threatened by the way I dance. Damn it, why'd I have to go showin' off like that? Now I'm all over his radar. Stupid!'
jokes.setup: Jeremy is trying to avoid going to the Cleary estate; he's looking for reasons
jokes.punchline: The pivot from legitimate concern (taxes) to absurd vanity ('he's threatened by the way I dance') to self-recrimination ('stupid!') is a classic Vaughn anxiety spiral — escalating irrationality delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: One of Vaughn's best moments in the reel. The comedic architecture is: plausible fear (taxes) → narcissistic leap (dancing threat) → self-blame (stupid!) — each beat more irrational and funnier than the last. The character integration is near-perfect: this specific flavor of anxious narcissism could ONLY be Jeremy. The escalation from paranoid but reasonable to 'he's jealous of my dancing' is a great comedic gear-shift.

jokes.text: John: 'You're not that good a dancer.' Jeremy: 'Oh, please! You and I both know I'm a phenomenal dancer. Now I know you're lying through your teeth!'
jokes.setup: Jeremy has claimed the Secretary is threatened by his dancing
jokes.punchline: John's gentle reality check is met with Jeremy's completely unironic insistence on his own phenomenal dancing, and his accusation that John is the liar, not him
jokes.explanation: 'Now I know you're lying through your teeth!' is the best button — Jeremy's self-delusion is so complete that John's honest assessment becomes the lie. Great character consistency and delivery.

jokes.text: Jeremy and John's escalating 'lock it up' argument — 'You lock it up.' / 'No, you lock it up.' / 'Lock it up. Lock it up.'
jokes.setup: Both men are arguing about whether to stay or leave
jokes.punchline: The 'lock it up' exchange devolves into a meaningless verbal loop where the phrase loses all authority and becomes pure competitive noise — a perfect expression of their co-dependent dynamic
jokes.explanation: The circular argument is a good character dynamic beat — neither man has real authority over the other, so their commands neutralize each other. Functional buddy-comedy texture.

jokes.text: Jeremy: 'She's like a kid at Toys R Us. I can't be around it.' / 'Get off your high horse. Stop judging people. You take off the white wig and you stop judging me.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy is complaining about Gloria's clinginess and John's moral stance
jokes.punchline: 'You take off the white wig and you stop judging me' — Jeremy accuses John of wearing a metaphorical white wig of judgment, which is an absurdly specific image for hypocrisy that only Vaughn could deliver
jokes.explanation: 'Take off the white wig and stop judging me' is a vivid, specific metaphor for moral superiority that feels uniquely Jeremy — chaotic, visual, and somehow logical within his worldview. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Jeremy's list of reasons not to go: 'If you want to hang out with Claire, the boyfriend and Cybill, by all means.' / 'He'd love you to come!' / Gloria materializes from nowhere: 'Yes! Yes! Baba ganoush!'
jokes.setup: Jeremy is making his final case not to go to the estate
jokes.punchline: Gloria appears at exactly the worst moment, confirming all of Jeremy's worst fears, and her 'Yes! Yes! Baba ganoush!' — a completely inexplicable victory exclamation — is the comedic cherry
jokes.explanation: 'Baba ganoush!' as a celebration exclamation is an inspired choice — it's the right amount of random, food-based, and unexpectedly ethnic-deli for a preppy secretary's daughter to say when excited. The timing of her appearance (literally proving Jeremy's fears true in real time) is excellent structure. High quotability — 'baba ganoush' as pure celebration energy has comedic afterlife.

jokes.text: John: 'You take off the white wig, and you stop judging me.' (to Jeremy about judging people)
jokes.setup: Jeremy says he 'can't be around' someone who's a 'nut job' (Gloria), positioning himself as the sane one.
jokes.punchline: John tells him to take off the white wig (part of his costume/fake identity) before passing judgment — highlighting the absurdity of a wedding crasher calling anyone else a nut job.
jokes.explanation: A sharp meta-comment on Jeremy's hypocrisy. The white wig detail is specific and funny — referencing the disguise they're wearing while arguing about normalcy. Good economy.

jokes.text: Jeremy: 'I don't have any bodily fluids left in me' — describing what Gloria did to him below deck
jokes.setup: Jeremy has arrived at the estate looking wrecked; John asks if he's okay
jokes.punchline: 'She took me below deck for 45 minutes. I don't have any bodily fluids left in me.' — the frank horror of sexual exhaustion delivered as a trauma report rather than a brag
jokes.explanation: Good dark comedy — a man who treats sex as conquest is now describing it as depletion. The 45-minute specificity and 'bodily fluids left in me' as a medical-style assessment of damage is the comedic texture. The inversion of the predator becoming prey is the character note.

jokes.text: Mr. Cleary invites them to touch football: 'Don't forget to stretch, guys. We're gonna be on the field in 10.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy has just said he has no bodily fluids left; both men are physically and emotionally depleted
jokes.punchline: The Secretary's breezy 'Don't forget to stretch, guys' — a cheerful athletic challenge issued to two men in deeply compromised physical/psychological states — sets up the next sequence's comedic premise
jokes.explanation: A setup joke for the football sequence — the comedy is in the ironic contrast between the men's depleted state and the perky athletic invitation. Functional plot-comedy beat, not a standout in its own right.

jokes.text: 'Are you ready for some football? You want the noise brought on you? 'Cause here it comes.' / 'The what?' / 'The noise brought on you, 'cause here it comes.' / 'Just hike the ball, nut job.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy hypes himself up with trash talk before a casual family touch-football game, inventing the nonsensical phrase 'the noise brought on you'
jokes.punchline: John deflates the entire thing with 'Just hike the ball, nut job.' — the trash talk is so incoherent it demands immediate shutdown
jokes.explanation: The comedy comes from Jeremy's total commitment to made-up bravado ('the noise brought on you') and John's weary shutdown. The invented phrase is specific enough to feel like character — only Vince Vaughn's motormouth character would say something this confidently meaningless. Good character integration.

jokes.text: 'Crab cakes and football! That's what Maryland does!'
jokes.setup: Jeremy catches a touchdown pass in a low-stakes family football game and celebrates
jokes.punchline: The celebration is a non sequitur conflating Maryland cuisine with athletic achievement — the specificity of 'crab cakes' as a victory cry is the joke
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in this reel. The absurd specificity — crab cakes as a pride point — combined with Jeremy's pure exuberance makes it land hard. It's economical and highly original. The randomness is earned by Jeremy's character (over-the-top enthusiasm for everything). A genuine crowd-pleaser with rewatchability.

jokes.text: 'What happened, Toast?' / 'I think he's on steroids. It was like trying to cover a fuckin' racehorse.'
jokes.setup: Sack (the antagonist, Claire's boyfriend) got beaten on a play by Jeremy in the family football game
jokes.punchline: His player blaming steroids rather than admitting Jeremy simply outplayed him — the excuse is both absurd and character-revealing
jokes.explanation: Functional gag — the racehorse simile is funny and the steroid accusation fits the macho absurdity of the game. Doesn't reach beyond competent, but earns its place.

jokes.text: John instructs Jeremy to throw an intentional interception to Claire to make her 'feel good' and 'gets them foamy.' Jeremy responds: 'John, I was first team, all-state. I can put the ball wherever I want to. I'll make it rain out here.'
jokes.setup: John asks Jeremy to deliberately throw to Claire to charm her — a low-stakes, underhanded request
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's response is hilariously disproportionate — invoking his high school all-state credentials and 'make it rain' for what is essentially deliberate incompetence
jokes.explanation: Jeremy's ego is perfectly captured here — invoking athletic credentials to brag about his ability to miss on purpose. 'I'll make it rain' is a great Vince Vaughn line. High character integration.

jokes.text: 'Oh, you're gonna cover me?' / 'Like white on rice.' / 'I like my odds here. I'm gonna give you a little warning, I'm going downtown.'
jokes.setup: Sack confidently declares he'll cover Jeremy 'like white on rice'
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's chirpy counter-trash-talk — 'I'm going downtown' — in a family touch football game is comic in its over-seriousness
jokes.explanation: Competent escalation of the trash-talk running gag. The comedy is in the absurd gravity both men bring to a family game.

jokes.text: 'John! Red seven!' / 'What? I don't know what red seven means.' / 'Hot route!' / 'I don't... w-what is hot route?' / 'Will you just go stand on the other side, please?' / 'Are you runnin' away from me?' / 'No! I'm just gettin' over here.' / 'You scared?'
jokes.setup: Sack barks football terminology at John as though they're in the NFL
jokes.punchline: John's baffled, earnest non-comprehension of 'red seven' and 'hot route' deflates Sack's macho posturing, then John turns it into a taunt ('Are you runnin' away from me? You scared?')
jokes.explanation: Owen Wilson's bewildered innocence against Sack's alpha-male football talk is a good comedic pairing. The pivot where John starts taunting him ('You scared?') is a nice structural beat.

jokes.text: Jeremy sacks Sack (or someone) and shouts: 'Boo-ya! That's what we call a sack lunch! Num-num-num-num-num-num!'
jokes.setup: Jeremy makes a big defensive play
jokes.punchline: 'Sack lunch' — a pun on the player Sack's name and a sack in football, delivered with absurd vocal celebration
jokes.explanation: The 'sack lunch' pun is elegant — it works on two levels (the player's name, the football term) and the 'num-num-num' noise is pure Vince Vaughn id. Character-specific and energetic.

jokes.text: 'Big tree fall hard, right? How many fingers I got up? Come on, Pepe, how many fingers I got up?'
jokes.setup: Someone (presumably Sack) has been knocked down hard
jokes.punchline: Jeremy mockingly crouches over the fallen man, delivering 'Big tree fall hard' (mocking his size/masculinity) then doing a fake medical check with 'Pepe' (a dismissive, slightly absurd nickname)
jokes.explanation: The 'Pepe' nickname is an odd, funny choice — the arbitrary condescension of a fake medical concern while taunting. Good Jeremy energy.

jokes.text: Jeremy can't breathe — he's down. His injury is real, but: 'Well, serves him right after that throw.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy appears to be genuinely hurt and struggling to breathe on the field
jokes.punchline: Sack's immediate, callous 'serves him right after that throw' — prioritizing football pride over human concern
jokes.explanation: Perfect character moment for Sack — his sociopathic competitiveness is revealed in one perfect line. Economy is excellent; it says everything about his villainy without belaboring it.

jokes.text: 'Hey! Baba ganoush!' (Secretary Cleary calling to John)
jokes.setup: Secretary Cleary needs to get John's attention on the football field
jokes.punchline: He calls him 'Baba ganoush' — a completely inexplicable Middle Eastern dip used as a nickname, delivered with total authority
jokes.explanation: One of the funnier non-sequiturs in the reel. The Secretary of State using 'baba ganoush' as a casual nickname for a stranger is the right kind of absurd — it also implies a certain oblivious patrician power. Highly quotable and rewatchable.

jokes.text: Secretary Cleary: 'Five generations of Lodge family breeding.' (Explaining why Jeremy is athletic)
jokes.setup: John wonders what got into Jeremy (who is performing well under the guise of being from the Lodge family)
jokes.punchline: The Secretary attributes Jeremy's athleticism to 'five generations of Lodge family breeding' — pompously crediting aristocratic genetics for the crasher's performance, completely oblivious
jokes.explanation: The joke works on the dramatic irony of the crashing premise — the Secretary is unknowingly complimenting a fraud by crediting a fictional bloodline. Good character work for the pompous father figure.

jokes.text: Todd (the gay son) is asked to play football. 'You must be joking.' Secretary: 'It wouldn't kill you to play some competitive sports once in a while, would it?' Todd: 'Well, would that make you love me?'
jokes.setup: The Secretary cheerfully calls Todd into the football game
jokes.punchline: Todd's devastatingly direct 'Well, would that make you love me?' — cutting through the patriarchal sports ritual with raw emotional truth, played for uncomfortable laughs
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in this reel. The setup (father cheerfully insisting on sports) is a recognizable father-son cliché, but Todd's response is a perfect subversion — it's simultaneously funny, cutting, and genuinely sad. The economy is exceptional: six words that expose an entire dysfunctional relationship. The Secretary's 'Pfft. Jesus.' response seals it. This approaches the 8.0 anchor benchmark in structure and character integration.

jokes.text: 'Red moon dog 7-11! / 42, 30-teen!'
jokes.setup: John tries to call plays like a real quarterback at the line
jokes.punchline: '30-teen' is a made-up number — John doesn't know real football signals and is just improvising nonsense with confidence
jokes.explanation: '30-teen' is the standout comic invention here — a small but perfectly formed absurdist number. The line reading of confident gibberish is what makes it work.

jokes.text: 'Nature versus nurture, Lodge. Nature always wins.' (Said over Jeremy lying on the ground again)
jokes.setup: Jeremy has been knocked down again by what appears to be uncontrollable aggression from the same player
jokes.punchline: The Secretary delivers a philosophical verdict ('Nature always wins') while crediting the Lodge bloodline — again, completely missing that Jeremy is a fraud
jokes.explanation: A callback that doubles down on the patrician bloodline joke. Works but slightly less impactful than the original since the premise has been established.

jokes.text: 'If I had any air in my lungs, I'd scream at you!' / 'Oh, now you're gonna blame me? 'Cause you're not athletic enough to stay on your two feet?' / 'I hate you.' / 'Let's take a daiquiri time-out.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy, on the ground and gasping, tries to argue with John about what just happened
jokes.punchline: The escalating absurdity of arguing while unable to breathe, then John defusing the whole thing with 'Let's take a daiquiri time-out'
jokes.explanation: 'Daiquiri time-out' is a perfect John line — casually dissolving a macho football argument with a cocktail suggestion. It captures Owen Wilson's character (charming, slightly checked out) in three words.

jokes.text: 'Let's take a daiquiri time-out.'
jokes.setup: The football game has devolved into genuine injury and argument
jokes.punchline: The civilized suggestion of a daiquiri break to resolve a physical altercation is a perfect tonal shift — the wedding-crasher ease in wealthy social situations
jokes.explanation: Clean, economical comedic beat — the contrast of violence/daiquiris is funny and John's social smoothness is well-deployed here.

jokes.text: Jeremy: 'Oh, Jesus Christ. It burns.' Gloria treating his cut: 'You want me to blow on it?' / Jeremy: 'No. No no no. No no no. No, I don't need any blowing. I'm good.'
jokes.setup: Gloria innocently offers to blow on Jeremy's wound to ease the sting
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's panicked over-refusal — 'No, I don't need any blowing. I'm good, I'm good' — reveals he's interpreting the offer sexually and trying desperately to stay composed
jokes.explanation: Classic double entendre setup with Jeremy's frantic response being the real joke. His over-correction ('I don't need any blowing') is funnier than a simple reaction.

jokes.text: Gloria: 'Jeremy, I'm not wearing any panties.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy is trying to stay composed while Gloria tends to his wound
jokes.punchline: Gloria casually drops the panty revelation mid-first-aid — an abrupt, context-free sexual disclosure that completely torpedoes the innocent scene
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic economy — the joke is entirely in the delivery and timing. Gloria's transformation from shy virgin to overtly sexual aggressor is the running character joke of this whole section. The mid-first-aid context makes it funnier than if it were delivered in a neutral situation.

jokes.text: Jeremy: 'Uh, yeah, that's fun, yeah. That's fun. Okay, Gloria, could you just stop for...' (panicked, overwhelmed)
jokes.setup: Gloria is apparently touching/groping Jeremy in some way after the panties revelation
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's verbal loop ('that's fun, that's fun, that's funny, that's funny') trying to laugh it off while clearly terrified — the stutter-loop is the joke
jokes.explanation: Vince Vaughn's flustered word-loop is a good performance joke. The escalating repetition of 'that's fun/funny' as his composure disintegrates is a character-specific comedic mode.

jokes.text: Randolph the butler appears: 'Don't you worry, Miss Gloria. Mum's the word.' — has apparently witnessed the whole scene
jokes.setup: Jeremy is in a compromising situation with Gloria
jokes.punchline: The butler materializes out of nowhere, clearly having watched everything, and offers conspiratorial silence — his discreet presence implies a household where this is normal
jokes.explanation: The silent butler who appears at the worst moment and offers complicit silence is a great comic device. His existence implies this is routine in the Cleary household, which is funnier than any explicit explanation.

jokes.text: Jeremy: 'Just like eight hours ago you were a shy little virgin, and now you're not wearing any panties. I'm just trying to catch up with you here.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy tries to rationally address Gloria's sexual transformation
jokes.punchline: The comic understatement of 'I'm just trying to catch up with you here' as a descriptor for her going from Virgin Mary to aggressive seductress overnight
jokes.explanation: Good callback that consolidates the film's running Gloria gag. The reasonable-man-in-an-unreasonable-situation voice (Jeremy trying to 'catch up') is Vince Vaughn's sweet spot.

jokes.text: Gloria: 'You do that to me.' Jeremy: 'I do what... no no no. Where's my little friend? He's tired. He's tired. He's in time-out. He's in time-out.'
jokes.setup: Gloria grabs at Jeremy sexually and asks where his 'little friend' is
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's euphemistic descriptions for his penis — 'He's tired,' 'He's in time-out' — as though it's a misbehaving pet he's responsible for
jokes.explanation: 'He's in time-out' is a genuinely original euphemism — treating one's own penis as a wayward child being disciplined is a funny, specific, and quotable construct. High character integration (Vince Vaughn's flustered motormouth persona).

jokes.text: Jeremy: 'Dry hump me up and down the field all afternoon. My leg's cut and bleeding. I'm just... I'm not really in the mood for this.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy is trying to explain why he's not interested in Gloria's advances
jokes.punchline: The list of grievances ('dry hump me up and down the field') that makes the football game sound like a sexual assault, culminating in a completely reasonable 'I'm not in the mood'
jokes.explanation: 'Dry hump me up and down the field' as a description of being tackled/covered in football is a great double-meaning that recontextualizes the earlier game. Good economy and Vince Vaughn specificity.

jokes.text: Gloria: 'My father warned me about people like you, Jeremy. I'm just another notch on your belt!'
jokes.setup: Jeremy is trying to slow things down; Gloria's emotions escalate wildly
jokes.punchline: Gloria performing romantic devastation over a man who is desperately trying to AVOID sleeping with her — the total inversion of the usual seduction dynamic
jokes.explanation: The inversion of the classic 'I'm just another notch' trope — here said by the aggressor to the person refusing her — is sharp writing. It makes Gloria both funny and slightly unhinged.

jokes.text: Jeremy's speech to calm Gloria: 'I'm feeling very strongly that we're only starting to express ourselves in a physical, sexual-specifically way.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy needs to talk Gloria down from a meltdown while also not triggering more aggression
jokes.punchline: 'sexual-specifically' — Jeremy inventing corporate-speak pseudo-therapy jargon to navigate an insane romantic situation; the bureaucratic register is completely wrong for the moment
jokes.explanation: 'Sexual-specifically' is a perfectly Vince-Vaughn-ism — the kind of confident corporate-therapy non-word that only his character would deploy in this situation. High character integration.

jokes.text: Gloria: 'Jeremy, you're amazing!' / Jeremy: 'Oh God, I think you're amazing.' / Gloria: 'Oh my God, don't ever leave me.' / Jeremy: 'Ever.' / Gloria: 'Good! 'Cause I'd find you.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy's speech works — Gloria goes from hysterical to adoring. The scene reaches a sweet romantic moment...
jokes.punchline: 'Good! 'Cause I'd find you.' — Gloria flips from declaration of love to casual stalker threat, delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the reel. The structure is near-perfect: the scene lulls the audience into a fake tender moment, and then 'I'd find you' lands as a completely unexpected escalation into menace. The deadpan delivery of a stalker threat as a romantic reassurance is both hilarious and deeply character-specific to Gloria. High quotability, strong rewatch value. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor benchmark.

jokes.text: Todd's confessional: 'Of course like all kids, I had imaginary friends, but not just one. I had hundreds and hundreds and all of them from different backgrounds who spoke different languages. And one of them, whose name was Caleb, he spoke a magical language that only I could understand.'
jokes.setup: A quiet, sincere-seeming confessional from Todd
jokes.punchline: What begins as a relatable anecdote ('like all kids, I had imaginary friends') escalates to hundreds of imaginary friends with specific demographics and a magical private language — delivered as though completely normal
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully strange character monologue. The escalation from 'imaginary friends' (relatable) to 'hundreds and hundreds from different backgrounds' (absurd) to one with a private magical language is perfectly constructed. Todd's character (repressed, eccentric, damaged) is entirely captured in this brief riff. Strong originality — this is specific writing, not generic comedy.

jokes.text: Jeremy to Secretary Cleary: 'You know, she's not just another notch on the old belt.' / Secretary: 'I don't even wear a belt. Beltless.' / Jeremy: 'I'm a very powerful man.' / Secretary: 'Yes, you are.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy tries to reassure the Secretary that his intentions toward Gloria are honorable, using the phrase 'notch on the belt'
jokes.punchline: The Secretary takes it completely literally ('I don't even wear a belt. Beltless.') — a non sequitur that completely derails Jeremy's earnest speech, then Jeremy's bizarre power claim and the Secretary's sincere affirmation
jokes.explanation: A great exchange. 'Beltless' is a perfectly deadpan non sequitur delivered by a man of enormous power who takes a figure of speech literally. Then 'I'm a very powerful man' out of nowhere — and the Secretary's earnest 'Yes, you are' — creates a surreal affirmation loop. The Secretary is played as genially oblivious throughout and this crystallizes his character comedically.

jokes.text: John is so bored by Sack's environmental story that he breaks down and grabs the eyedrops, then hands them over: 'Give me the eyedrops.' / 'Thank you.'
jokes.setup: John has been trying to beat Sack 'honorably' and resist drugging him; Sack's story about wiping oil off a sea otter is crushingly boring
jokes.punchline: John's moral stand crumbles mid-story — the moment he grabs the drops is the punchline to 'I can beat this guy. Let's be honorable for once.'
jokes.explanation: Very well-structured delayed payoff — the setup of 'I want to be honorable' followed by the story of the otter's whiskers being described in excruciating detail, culminating in John wordlessly grabbing the drops, is a textbook escalation-and-break structure. The timing across the scene is excellent.

jokes.text: Sack: '...an organic scallop farm right off the coast of Nattachoke. Actually, Sack got the Governor to subsidize part of the project. And now it's the state's only self-sustaining scallop farm. Say that five times, fast. You can't do it. Self-sustaining...'
jokes.setup: Sack explains his scallop farm during the dinner, referring to himself in the third person and then immediately derailing into a tongue-twister challenge
jokes.punchline: Third-person self-reference ('Sack got the Governor to subsidize') and then the narcissistic pivot to a tongue-twister challenge about his own achievement — the self-satisfaction is the joke
jokes.explanation: Third-person self-reference is a classic narcissist tell, and the tongue-twister gambit ('Say that five times fast') as a form of self-congratulation is well-observed. Good character writing for Sack.

jokes.text: Jeremy: 'Maybe I'll actually try some when I get the sensation back in my face from the... football game.' / Sack: 'Again, Jeremy, I'm sorry. I just, you know, I have this damn competitive streak. Um... I'm seeing a Buddhist about it. Not just any Buddhist. His Holiness, the Dalai Lama. He's a good friend.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy references the injuries Sack inflicted during the football game; Sack performs an apology
jokes.punchline: Sack's escalating apology: I'm seeing a Buddhist → not just any Buddhist → the Dalai Lama → 'He's a good friend.' — the name-drop arms race as an apology is a perfect character riff
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure is clean: apology → therapy → famous therapist → 'good friend' — each beat more self-aggrandizing than the last. 'He's a good friend' as a casual qualifier for the Dalai Lama is a great button. Classic status-comedy.

jokes.text: 'I just, you know, I have this damn competitive streak. Um... I'm seeing a Buddhist about it. Not just any Buddhist. His Holiness, the Dalai Lama. He's a good friend.'
jokes.setup: Sack is apologizing for his violent behavior in the football game
jokes.punchline: The name-drop escalates from 'a Buddhist' to 'the Dalai Lama... he's a good friend' — the casual intimacy with the world's most famous spiritual leader as a brag
jokes.explanation: Excellent character-establishment joke. The escalation from 'a Buddhist' to 'his Holiness, the Dalai Lama... he's a good friend' is perfectly structured — the pause before 'He's a good friend' is where the laugh is. Very Sack-specific: even his therapy is a status symbol.

jokes.text: Jeremy derailing Sack's interruption: John asks 'Hey, Sack, how long have you and Claire been seeing each other?' mid-Jeremy's grievance monologue, cutting him off perfectly.
jokes.setup: Jeremy is mid-speech about seeing an orthopedist for his injuries; Sack is name-dropping
jokes.punchline: John cuts the entire conversation off with a conversational redirect — his social timing (pivoting to romance/Claire) is both strategic and comic in its bluntness
jokes.explanation: More of a plot beat than a pure joke, but John's strategic redirect — deployed exactly when Sack is mid-brag — has comic timing. Functional.

jokes.text: Jeremy's escalating counter-rant about the orthopedist: 'Not just any orthopedist, I'm gonna see a Dr. Epstein who specializes in—' — immediately interrupted by John changing the subject
jokes.setup: Sack has just done the 'not just any Buddhist' escalation; Jeremy tries to do the same thing with his injury complaint
jokes.punchline: John cuts him off mid-sentence to redirect the conversation — Jeremy's attempt to match Sack's name-dropping game gets instantly derailed
jokes.explanation: Smart structural joke — Jeremy mirrors Sack's rhetorical move exactly ('Not just any orthopedist') and John kills it. The interruption is funnier because we can see where Jeremy was going. Good economy in the callback.

jokes.text: 'And then of course, you can challenge the Klingons for interstellar domination, right?' — Jeremy to the Secretary after the speech about two great American families uniting
jokes.setup: Secretary Cleary delivers a grandiose speech about two great American families (Clearys and Lodges) finally uniting through Claire and Sack's marriage
jokes.punchline: Jeremy deflates the pomposity by analogizing it to Star Trek — 'challenge the Klingons for interstellar domination' — reducing dynastic megalomania to sci-fi nerd-dom
jokes.explanation: A sharp deflation of aristocratic pomposity with a pop-culture comparison that makes the Secretary's self-importance look ridiculous. The specificity of 'Klingons' over a generic sci-fi reference is good craft.

jokes.text: Secretary Cleary to John: 'I saw you on the dance floor. You move pretty good.' John: 'Oh. Thanks a lot. I... really just got lucky. I was more in the zone than anything else. It was the booze dancing.'
jokes.setup: The Secretary of State compliments John on his dancing
jokes.punchline: 'It was the booze dancing.' — John's perfectly honest, self-deprecating explanation that credits alcohol as the actual dancer
jokes.explanation: 'The booze dancing' is a genuinely good coinage — economical, honest, and very Owen Wilson. The Secretary taking the compliment seriously and John gently dismissing it with alcohol credit is well-played.

jokes.text: Someone asks how the crashers are connected to the family: 'Uncle Ned's kids.' / 'You know... Uncle Ned?' / 'Aunt Liz's brother. Ned and Liz.' / 'Hmm. No, I don't know.'
jokes.setup: Someone at the dinner table asks how John and Jeremy know the family
jokes.punchline: Their cover story of 'Uncle Ned' leads to an awkward escalation of specificity ('Aunt Liz's brother') that still results in nobody recognizing the name — the crashers' brazen invention of relatives they don't have
jokes.explanation: A classic wedding-crasher-premise joke — the bluffing escalation followed by a blank stare. Good cringe structure even if not exceptional.

jokes.text: Jeremy's explanation of his 'venture capitalist' work: taking wool from sheep and turning it into thread for homeless people to sew into cloth into shirts and pants for other homeless people to sell...
jokes.setup: Jeremy is asked to give an example of an 'ethically and morally defensible' company they invest in
jokes.punchline: His description becomes increasingly circular and vague — wool to thread to cloth to shirts to pants — a never-ending loop of homeless-people-helping-homeless-people that never quite makes economic sense
jokes.explanation: Jeremy improvising a fake ethical business plan that becomes an absurdist circular economy is excellent Vince Vaughn verbal comedy. The repetition ('make it into cloth, which they in turn sew, then... make some shirts and pants') mirrors real people who can't stop talking when they're lying. High character integration.

jokes.text: 'Someone has to pay for the, uh, lap dances for the big guy here.' (Jeremy crediting John with expense account abuse)
jokes.setup: Jeremy is explaining the profits from his fake ethical company
jokes.punchline: He casually mentions the profit goes to lap dances for 'the big guy' (John) — a sudden, jarring pivot from socially-conscious business to strip club expenses
jokes.explanation: A quick pivot gag — the contrast between ethical corporate-speak and 'lap dances' is functional. John's reaction ('He's joking around. It feels so good when he jokes.') is the better part.

jokes.text: John: 'He's joking around. It feels so good when he jokes.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy just mentioned lap dances at a dinner with the Secretary of State
jokes.punchline: John's weirdly sincere, oddly intimate 'It feels so good when he jokes' — a non-reaction that doubles as a creepy endorsement, treating the moment as a heartwarming display of their friendship
jokes.explanation: Owen Wilson's calm sincerity covering what should be damage control is a great character beat. 'It feels so good when he jokes' is a strange, specific, quotable phrase — it has a slightly unsettling intimacy that lands perfectly.

jokes.text: 'Holy sh...' / 'Shirts & Pants. Holy Shirts & Pants.' / 'It's a little corny and obvious, but what do you get out of being subtle, right?'
jokes.setup: Someone asks what the company is called — Jeremy nearly blurts 'Holy shit' and John has to rescue with the company name
jokes.punchline: 'Holy Shirts & Pants' — the company name IS the near-expletive, an absurd and barely-hidden pun. Then Jeremy's instant meta-commentary 'It's a little corny and obvious, but what do you get out of being subtle?'
jokes.explanation: One of the more cleverly constructed jokes in the reel. The near-slip becomes the punchline, the punchline IS a pun, and then Jeremy's instant meta-defense of his own bad pun ('what do you get out of being subtle?') adds a third layer. The structure is excellent — three beats, each funnier than the last. High rewatch value because you catch the setup differently on rewatch.

jokes.text: Grandma Cleary on FDR's wife Eleanor Roosevelt: 'He was a doll. The wife, though, Eleanor... big dyke! Huge dyke! A real rug muncher! Looked like a big lesbian mule.'
jokes.setup: Grandma waxes nostalgic about FDR, the family's connection to Roosevelt-era Washington
jokes.punchline: The pivot from fond nostalgia ('He was a doll') to escalating slurs about Eleanor ('big dyke → huge dyke → rug muncher → lesbian mule') — the escalation of the attack and the absurdity of the final insult
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is entirely character-based — the contrast between Grandma's genteel setting and her escalating vulgarity. 'Lesbian mule' is an absurd construction that generates a laugh from its sheer specificity. Docked slightly on earned_vs_cheap because the slurs as comedy is a dated device — the laugh comes from the character's obliviousness rather than clever writing. The table's horrified reaction (implied) completes the joke.

jokes.text: Grandma: 'Somebody... somebody get me another Scotch for Christ sakes! I think I'm gonna go to bed.'
jokes.setup: Everyone at the table is mortified after Grandma's Eleanor Roosevelt tirade
jokes.punchline: Grandma's demand for more Scotch and casual declaration that she's going to bed — no remorse, no awareness, just continuing her evening as normal
jokes.explanation: A button on the grandma joke. The demand for Scotch mid-scandal is good character work but doesn't add much beyond what joke #44 already established.

jokes.text: 'Grandma, you can't talk like that, okay? It's not right.' — said with weary familiarity
jokes.setup: Grandma has just unloaded graphic slurs about Eleanor Roosevelt at the dinner table
jokes.punchline: Claire's correction is so measured and weary that it's clear this happens often — the 'okay? It's not right' has the cadence of a correction that has never once worked
jokes.explanation: Good reaction beat — the deflated normalcy of Claire's correction implies years of Grandma behavior. Functional rather than brilliant.

jokes.text: 'What an athlete. A tremendous competitor.' (Said over presumably the still-injured Jeremy or the football game aftermath)
jokes.setup: In the aftermath of the football game where Jeremy was repeatedly knocked down and hurt
jokes.punchline: The Secretary delivers a completely sincere athletic tribute to Jeremy — either sincerely or sarcastically, the gap between his evaluation and Jeremy's actual performance is funny
jokes.explanation: A mild callback gag. Works as a character note for the Secretary but doesn't generate much beyond a smile.

jokes.text: Secretary Cleary: 'Todd, I noticed that you haven't even touched your food yet.' / 'I don't eat meat or fish.' / Grandma: 'He's a homo.'
jokes.setup: The Secretary makes a perfectly innocent observation about Todd's eating
jokes.punchline: Grandma immediately interprets vegetarianism as a gay signifier — 'He's a homo' — with the same casual authority she used for Eleanor Roosevelt
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words ('He's a homo') after a completely unrelated observation about food. The logic jump (doesn't eat meat → gay) is so absurd and the delivery so authoritative that it lands hard. Grandma's consistent obliviousness makes this a callback payoff. Docked slightly on earned_vs_cheap for the same reasons as #44.

jokes.text: Mrs. Cleary (the mom): 'Mommy, let's not go there again.' / 'Actually, um, Todd is an amazing painter. He's going to the Rhode Island School of Design.'
jokes.setup: Grandma has just called Todd a homo at the dinner table
jokes.punchline: 'Let's not go there again' implies this has happened many times — the normalization of Grandma's bigotry as a repeated family drama, and the pivot to RISD as damage control
jokes.explanation: The 'again' is the joke — implying a repeated pattern of Grandma outbursts. Functional but not strong on its own.

jokes.text: John: 'That's really impressive, Rizdee.' (mispronouncing/slang-ifying RISD)
jokes.setup: Someone says Todd is going to the Rhode Island School of Design
jokes.punchline: John's knowing use of 'Rizdee' — the insider slang for RISD — signals he's culturally fluent in ways a fake family member might not be, and it's slightly odd/try-hard in context
jokes.explanation: Minor joke. The 'Rizdee' shows John's charm-through-knowledge but is a small beat. Not particularly funny on its own but establishes his social intelligence.

jokes.text: Todd: 'Dad used to think I'd be a political liability, you know, in case he ever ran for President.' Secretary: 'Now, Todd! Actually, truth be told, polling shows a majority of the American people would ultimately empathize with our situation.' Todd: 'What is our situation, Dad?!' Secretary: 'You're a homo.'
jokes.setup: Todd brings up his father's past concern that Todd's homosexuality could be a political liability
jokes.punchline: The Secretary's focus-grouped, pollster-calibrated defense of his gay son — 'polling shows a majority would empathize' — reduces a family relationship to electoral math. Then the Secretary defining 'our situation' as simply 'You're a homo' after all the diplomatic framing
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The Secretary's response — framing his son's sexuality as a political polling question — is both hilarious and devastatingly character-revealing. It shows him as someone who processes everything through political strategy. The structure is excellent: the diplomatic windup ('polling shows a majority would empathize with our situation') is immediately undercut by the brutal plainspokenness of 'You're a homo.' The gap between the sophisticated framing and the two-word punchline is perfect. High character integration — only this exact character delivers this joke. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor benchmark.

jokes.text: Grandma: 'Oh, for God sakes, William, put Mommy to bed already.' / Mrs. Cleary: 'Okay. Mommy, we've had a long day.' / Grandma: 'I can do it myself, asshole.'
jokes.setup: Everyone tries to manage Grandma after the Todd exchange
jokes.punchline: Grandma demanding to be put to bed, then snarling 'I can do it myself, asshole' the second Mrs. Cleary tries to help — the reflexive contrarianism of an entitled elder
jokes.explanation: 'I can do it myself, asshole' is a perfectly constructed contradiction — she just asked for help, then refused it with an insult. The reflexive aggression is a great button to the Grandma character arc through the dinner scene. Good economy.

jokes.text: Todd: 'I'll be in my room painting.' Secretary: 'You just go right ahead, Toddy.' Todd (muttered): 'Homo things.'
jokes.setup: Todd exits the dinner table after the humiliating homo exchange
jokes.punchline: Todd's self-deprecating/defiant 'Homo things' — said quietly, possibly to himself — is simultaneously sad, funny, and weirdly empowered
jokes.explanation: Two words that do enormous work. Todd reclaiming the slur by applying it to his own art ('homo things') is funny, painful, and character-specific. The economy is near-perfect — the entire Todd-father dynamic is compressed into this throwaway exit line. It earns its high score through perfect compression and character specificity. This is the kind of line that becomes a fan-favorite for the Todd character.

jokes.text: Mrs. Cleary to John: 'I just had my tits done. You like 'em?' John: 'Those... seem like lovely tits.'
jokes.setup: John has excused himself for some air; Mrs. Cleary intercepts him
jokes.punchline: John's completely baffled, polite, slightly formal response — 'Those... seem like lovely tits' — the word 'seem' doing enormous work as a gentleman's hedge on another man's wife's breasts
jokes.explanation: Owen Wilson's delivery makes this exceptional. 'Those... seem like lovely tits' is a masterclass in polite bewilderment — the pause before 'seem,' the formal register of 'lovely,' the hedging qualifier 'seem' applied to something you can apparently clearly see. It's both hilarious and very specifically Owen Wilson's character. High quotability.

jokes.text: Mrs. Cleary: 'William doesn't give a shit about my tits.' John: 'Well, darn him.'
jokes.setup: Mrs. Cleary overshares about her husband's indifference to her new implants
jokes.punchline: 'Well, darn him.' — John's perfectly chipper, mild-mannered disapproval as though someone has told him they cut in line, not complained about a sexless marriage
jokes.explanation: 'Well, darn him.' is a near-perfect comic response. The register mismatch — 'darn' as a response to marital sexual neglect — is pitch-perfect Owen Wilson. The word 'darn' in particular does all the work: too mild, too polite, too checked-out for the situation. Near-perfect economy (three words). Very quotable.

jokes.text: 'You've been playing cat and mouse with me ever since you came here.' / 'Mrs. Cleary, I don't...' / 'Call me Cat.' / 'Okay, Cat...' / 'Call me Kitty Cat.' / 'Okay, Kitty Cat, this feels borderline inappropriate...'
jokes.setup: Mrs. Cleary is coming on to John and assigns herself a name
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'Cat' to 'Kitty Cat' — she's negotiating her own nickname upward in real time, and John dutifully complies with each revision while trying to object to the situation
jokes.explanation: The 'Cat' to 'Kitty Cat' escalation is a clever bit — she interrupts her own seduction to upgrade her nickname. John's compliance ('Okay, Kitty Cat...') while simultaneously trying to register objection creates good layered comedy.

jokes.text: John: 'I'm sorry, Kitty Cat. Are you out of your fucking mind? I'm not letting you out of this room until you feel them.'
jokes.setup: Mrs. Cleary demands John feel her new implants
jokes.punchline: John's outburst ('Are you out of your fucking mind?') followed immediately by Mrs. Cleary continuing her demand completely unfazed — the juxtaposition of his justified horror and her calm insistence
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Mrs. Cleary's complete imperviousness to John's protest. His objection doesn't register at all — she just restates her demand. Good cringe escalation.

jokes.text: John (after feeling the implants): 'Wow, they feel really nice. Real orb-like.'
jokes.setup: John has been forced to feel Mrs. Cleary's implants against his will and is now obligated to comment
jokes.punchline: 'Real orb-like.' — the word 'orb' applied to breasts is the joke. It's so clinical, so astronomy-adjacent, so utterly wrong a word choice that it's hilarious
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the film. 'Orb-like' is a genuinely extraordinary word choice — clinical, slightly cosmic, entirely wrong for the situation, and yet delivered with Owen Wilson's breezy sincerity. The word does everything: it shows John trying to be polite in an impossible situation, using the most neutral descriptor he can find, and landing on something both funnier and stranger than any crude alternative. Near-perfect economy (four words). Highest quotability in the reel. This approaches the 8.0 anchor benchmark and arguably exceeds it.

jokes.text: Mrs. Cleary: 'Pervert.' (after John compliments her implants she forced him to feel)
jokes.setup: John has just complimented the implants Mrs. Cleary forced him to feel
jokes.punchline: 'Pervert.' — she calls him a pervert for enjoying something she compelled him to do. The complete inversion of agency is the joke
jokes.explanation: One word. That's the whole joke. Mrs. Cleary forces John to feel her implants, and when he compliments them, she calls him the pervert. The moral inversion is perfect and the economy is absolute. This is a great button — the entire absurdity of the scene is crystallized in a single word. One of the best-constructed moments in the reel.

jokes.text: Todd (to John in the hallway): 'Mom make you feel her tits?'
jokes.setup: John emerges from the room, clearly shaken
jokes.punchline: Todd asks the question with matter-of-fact familiarity — implying this is a known, recurring family situation that happens to guests. The casualness is the horror
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic beat. The question's matter-of-fact delivery implies this is known family behavior — Todd has seen it before, probably many times. The casualness transforms a weird incident into an indictment of the entire family's dysfunction. Economy is excellent: six words establish an entire horrifying family dynamic. High quotability and rewatch value as a callback payoff.

jokes.text: John: 'Todd, where are you going with this?' Todd: 'Just don't... don't say anything to my dad, though. Some friend of my sister's... said something to my dad a couple of years ago... he now lives in a shack in Guam. Not by choice.'
jokes.setup: Todd has just casually confirmed the mom forces guests to feel her implants
jokes.punchline: 'He now lives in a shack in Guam. Not by choice.' — the Secretary of State apparently sent someone to Guam for telling him about his wife's behavior, delivered as a friendly warning
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. 'He now lives in a shack in Guam. Not by choice.' is perfectly structured: the revelation (Guam), the quiet escalation ('Not by choice') — the two-beat delivery confirms the Secretary of State uses his power for petty revenge. The specificity of 'shack in Guam' is excellent. 'Not by choice' is a devastating qualifier that does enormous work in three words. High character integration for the Secretary.

jokes.text: 'Some friend of my sister's... said something to my dad a couple of years ago... he now lives in a shack in Guam. Not by choice.'
jokes.setup: Todd is explaining the consequences of telling Lodge about Mrs. Cleary's behavior
jokes.punchline: 'Not by choice.' — four word addendum that transforms 'lives in Guam' from a quirky detail into a threat. The implication is that Lodge had the man sent there.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The deadpan addition of 'Not by choice' is a perfect dark comedy button — it transforms the anecdote from merely weird to genuinely sinister, and the economy is superb. The implication of Lodge's mob-like power is revealed through Todd's total nonchalance. The pause before 'Not by choice' would land perfectly in a theater. Very high comparability to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: John: 'Stop kidding with me, Todd. You almost had me, come on.' (looking genuinely unsure)
jokes.setup: Todd has delivered the Guam warning completely straight-faced
jokes.punchline: John half-laughs it off as a joke, but his delivery ('You almost had me') shows he's not fully convinced — the ambiguity of whether it's a joke is the joke
jokes.explanation: A functional button on the Guam joke. John's uncertain laugh amplifies the horror of the previous line by suggesting it might all be true.

jokes.text: Jeremy to John: 'Claire's mom just made me grab her hooters.' John: 'Well, snap out of it! What? A hot, older woman made you feel her cans? Stop crying like a little girl.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy is traumatized by Mrs. Cleary's behavior and comes to John for support
jokes.punchline: John's completely unsympathetic response ('Snap out of it!') reframing sexual harassment as something Jeremy should be grateful for — the guy-code inversion where the victim is mocked for not enjoying it
jokes.explanation: John's bro-code response is funny in its obliviousness. The juxtaposition of Jeremy's genuine distress and John's incredulity ('a hot, older woman made you feel her cans?') captures the film's gender-comedy register well.

jokes.text: Jeremy: 'Why don't you try getting jacked off under the table in front of the whole damn family and have some real problems? Jackass.'
jokes.setup: John dismisses Jeremy's distress about Mrs. Cleary
jokes.punchline: Jeremy reveals he was masturbated under the dinner table in front of the entire family — delivered as a trump card in a complaint competition
jokes.explanation: A great escalation reveal — the dinner scene now gets retroactively funnier because we realize what was happening under the table. The reveal is well-timed and the 'and have some real problems?' framing is excellent. 'Jackass' as a button is perfect Vince Vaughn.

jokes.text: John: 'What were they like, anyway? They look pretty good. Are they real? Are they built for speed or for comfort? What you do with 'em? Motorboat? You play the motorboat? Ppppt! You motorboatin' son of a bitch. You old sailor, you! Where is she? She still in the house?'
jokes.setup: John just told Jeremy to stop crying about being groped by Mrs. Cleary, then immediately pivots to prurient curiosity
jokes.punchline: The rapid-fire escalation from casual inquiry ('What were they like?') to 'built for speed or comfort' to 'motorboat?' to full-on 'motorboatin' son of a bitch' in about ten seconds — John's hypocrisy exposed at speed
jokes.explanation: One of the most energetic comic monologues in the reel. The hypocrisy reveal (he just said 'snap out of it') combined with the escalating crudeness and the genuine enthusiasm of 'motorboatin' son of a bitch, you old sailor, you!' is classic Vince Vaughn — but delivered by Owen Wilson, which makes it funnier because John is usually more composed. 'Built for speed or for comfort' is a great recurring phrase. High quotability.

jokes.text: Jeremy: 'What is wrong with you?' John: 'What do you mean what's wrong with... what's wrong with you?' Jeremy: 'No, what's wrong with you?' John: 'No, what's wrong with you?' Jeremy: 'You're projecting.' John: 'Drop it.' Jeremy: 'You drop it! You stop projecting on me.'
jokes.setup: John's hypocrisy has been exposed; they're now bickering
jokes.punchline: The 'what's wrong with you / no, what's wrong with you' loop escalating to Jeremy using 'projecting' as a therapy term — the low-stakes psychobabble applied to a bicker about breast implants
jokes.explanation: The 'you're projecting' beat in a juvenile argument is a good bit — using therapy language as a weapon in a petty fight. The circular 'what's wrong with you' loop also captures their friendship dynamic.

jokes.text: Jeremy: 'Why don't you go enjoy yourself while I go ice my balls and spit up blood? Drop it!' John: 'Team player.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy is listing his physical complaints from the day
jokes.punchline: 'Ice my balls and spit up blood' as a to-do list delivered in a huff, then John's sarcastic 'Team player' as a final button — perfectly timed to deflate the dramatics
jokes.explanation: 'Ice my balls and spit up blood' is a great Vince Vaughn grievance list — specific, escalating, absurd. John's 'Team player' as the final word is a perfect one-word dismissal that lands as the button on the entire reel.

jokes.text: You banging the daughter and the grandma? How much jam you got, man?
jokes.setup: John has just finished carrying the drunken elderly grandmother to her room, an innocent if awkward act.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy interprets the scene as John having a sexual conquest with both the young daughter and the grandmother, coining the slang 'jam' for sexual prowess.
jokes.explanation: The 'jam' coinage is punchy and character-specific — Jeremy's hyperactive libido and misreading of every situation is perfectly distilled here. The economy is excellent: one line does the work of a whole misunderstanding. The grandmother angle adds a layer of absurdist escalation that earns a solid laugh.

jokes.text: Listen, man, the family dog lives downstairs. I can wake him up for you, if you like. His name is Snooky.
jokes.setup: Jeremy has just accused John of sleeping with both the daughter and the grandmother.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy escalates the absurdity by implying John might also want to hook up with the family dog — helpfully providing the dog's name.
jokes.explanation: The joke escalates an already absurd premise into genuine dark comedy territory. What makes it exceptional is the specific detail — the dog's name is Snooky. That specificity transforms a crude joke into a character moment: Jeremy's brain goes to such bizarre places so quickly, and he's already thought of the dog's name. It's comparable in structure to the 8.0 anchor: sharp, unexpected, highly quotable, perfect economy. The 'He be pushing 90!' capper seals it.

jokes.text: Just be gentle with her, okay? She be pushing 90!
jokes.setup: John desperately protests that nothing is happening with the grandmother.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy ignores the denial entirely and offers only the compassionate advice to 'be gentle' because she's nearly 90.
jokes.explanation: The callback capper lands because Jeremy completely ignores John's protest, treating the fantasy scenario as confirmed fact. The faux-tenderness ('be gentle with her') is the comedic inversion that sells it. Good character integration — this is precisely how Jeremy's delusional optimism operates.

jokes.text: Your family... are totally nuts. And guess what? I love it.
jokes.setup: Claire is self-conscious and apologizes for her 'a little strange' family. John seems to be gearing up for confirmation of that assessment.
jokes.punchline: Instead of agreeing with the negative, John pivots to genuine enthusiasm — 'I love it' — subverting the expected complaint.
jokes.explanation: A mild misdirection that works as a character beat — John's charm offensive is convincing enough to be funny. The comedy is light and comes from the warm sincerity of the reversal rather than any wit in the writing. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: You got the sweet little grandma who's really sweet with her, like, little, like, white hair, but then she's kinda mean. But you're like, 'Well, fuck it, she's so old, and she's not gonna change now.'
jokes.setup: John is enthusiastically describing what he loves about Claire's family to win her over.
jokes.punchline: His affectionate description of the grandmother includes the casually nihilistic 'fuck it, she's so old, she's not gonna change now' — a perfectly real observation delivered with cheerful energy.
jokes.explanation: The 'fuck it, she's so old' logic is genuinely funny because it's true — it's the unspoken social contract everyone has with elderly difficult relatives, articulated with cheerful profanity. The stumbling delivery ('like, little, like') is a bit loose but adds to John's charming-rambling quality.

jokes.text: You're like that crazy guest who thinks he's part of the family already... Doesn't sound that great. That sounds horrible. The crazy guest who thinks he's like a part of the family who's gonna say inappropriate stuff? What is that?
jokes.setup: Claire describes John as 'that crazy guest who thinks he's part of the family already' — intending it as a compliment.
jokes.punchline: John, breaking character momentarily, points out how horrible that description actually sounds, turning her intended flattery into an accidental insult.
jokes.explanation: A smart little reversal — the character catches that what she said sounds terrible on paper. The escalating repetition of the description ('crazy guest who thinks he's like part of the family who's gonna say inappropriate stuff') adds comedic momentum. Good banter structure.

jokes.text: Well, Claire, um... my head's buried in a toilet. What do you think? Why don't you do the math, okay?
jokes.setup: Claire finds Sack with his head in a toilet and asks 'Are you okay?'
jokes.punchline: Sack responds with withering contempt — 'my head's buried in a toilet. What do you think? Why don't you do the math' — an aggressively sarcastic non-answer that reveals his terrible personality even in vulnerability.
jokes.explanation: Strong character integration — Sack's nastiness is consistent whether he's in power or sick on the floor. 'Do the math' as a dismissal to a simple welfare check is a funny deployment of corporate-bro condescension. Works to advance characterization while generating a laugh.

jokes.text: Yeah, you can just cut that psychobabble bullshit that your mom tells you, okay? ... I think I might get vulnerable again.
jokes.setup: Claire tells Sack 'it's okay to be vulnerable sometimes' — offering genuine comfort.
jokes.punchline: Sack dismisses her emotional support as 'psychobabble bullshit' from her mother, then immediately uses 'vulnerable' as a euphemism for vomiting — 'I think I might get vulnerable again.'
jokes.explanation: The twist of using 'vulnerable' as a vomiting euphemism right after dismissing the emotional meaning of that word is sharp and character-specific. It's the kind of wordplay-within-character that elevates a gross joke. The hypocrisy lands. 'Get vulnerable again' is genuinely quotable.

jokes.text: Baby, I started thinking about what you said before and I think the problem is I am not being adventurous enough for you!
jokes.setup: Jeremy hears his door open in the dark and panics. Gloria has taken something Jeremy said — presumably a complaint or deflection — and interpreted it as a request for more sexual adventurousness.
jokes.punchline: The punchline is implicit: whatever 'adventurous' means in this context is clearly terrifying to Jeremy, as evidenced by his immediate horrified protest.
jokes.explanation: A solid cringe setup — Gloria's misinterpretation escalating into something ominous works well as a running gag payoff. The horror in Jeremy's immediate denial sells the comedy.

jokes.text: Gloria, I am pretty sure that is not what I've been saying to you.
jokes.setup: Gloria announces she's been inspired by Jeremy's words to be more 'adventurous.'
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's response — 'I am pretty sure that is not what I've been saying to you' — is a masterpiece of understatement and terrified politeness. The 'pretty sure' hedge is perfect.
jokes.explanation: The 'pretty sure' is the comedy — Jeremy is so afraid of Gloria that even correcting her obvious misreading is hedged into oblivion. It's behaviorally specific and very funny as a character beat. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Gloria: 'I'm gonna make all your fantasies come true.' Long pause as Jeremy tries to respond, then she says 'I love you.' Cut to black.
jokes.setup: Jeremy is trying to dissuade Gloria; she cuts him off with a declaration of fantasy fulfillment
jokes.punchline: 'I love you' — the declaration of love mid-assault, implying total lack of self-awareness; followed by cut to black implying the horror of what follows
jokes.explanation: The 'I love you' landing before the cut to black is excellent comedic economy — it simultaneously conveys Gloria's delusional emotional investment and the horror of what Jeremy is about to endure, without showing any of it. The gap between her tenderness and the situation's violence is the joke. The cut to black amplifies it perfectly.

jokes.text: It's not Gloria. / We had a moment at the dinner table, didn't we?
jokes.setup: Jeremy's room is visited again in the night. He assumes it's Gloria returning and says 'Gloria, go to sleep, honey.' Then a male voice corrects him.
jokes.punchline: It's Todd — the brother — who insists they 'had a moment at the dinner table.' This is a complete misdirection: the audience expected another Gloria attack; instead Jeremy now has a second nocturnal pursuer.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely surprising pivot that earns its impact. The setup of 'Gloria, go to sleep, honey' creates the expectation of a Gloria gag, then violates it with a new and worse problem. 'We had a moment at the dinner table' is delivered with such earnestness that it's deeply funny — Todd's completely sincere belief in this connection is the engine of the joke. Character integration is strong: Todd's delusion is the punchline.

jokes.text: I made you a painting. / What? / I call the painting 'Celebration.' It's sexual and violent. I thought you might like it.
jokes.setup: Todd has shown up in Jeremy's room claiming they had a romantic moment. Jeremy is bewildered.
jokes.punchline: Todd presents a painting called 'Celebration' that he describes as 'sexual and violent' — with no apparent irony — and offers it as a romantic gesture.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The title 'Celebration' paired with the descriptor 'sexual and violent' is a perfect absurdist juxtaposition — these words have no business being in the same sentence about a gift painting, and the deadpan 'I thought you might like it' treats this as perfectly normal courtship. The specificity (a named painting, with an aesthetic description) elevates it far above a generic 'weird gay guy' joke. It becomes a memorable character-defining moment for Todd. Genuinely comparable to the high-end anchor examples in structure and quotability.

jokes.text: Jeremy's single 'No.' in response to the painting
jokes.setup: Todd presents the painting 'Celebration' — 'sexual and violent' — as a romantic overture.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's flat, singular 'No.' is the perfect straight-man response to absurdity — complete, unadorned, final.
jokes.explanation: One word, maximally effective. The economy score is as high as it gets — there's nothing to cut. It works as a reaction beat that punctuates joke #13 perfectly. It's a beat, not a standalone joke, but it earns its own entry because the timing and delivery are the payload.

jokes.text: No no no no. Hide hide hide! / They need to know about us. / No no no. Hide, please. ... Let's play tummy sticks! / What's tummy sticks? / I don't want to play tummy sticks! Get in the closet.
jokes.setup: Someone is coming and Jeremy frantically tries to get Todd to hide. Todd wants to come out about their supposed relationship.
jokes.punchline: Todd suggests 'Let's play tummy sticks' — an invented sexual act whose name alone is horrifying — mid-crisis. Jeremy's bewildered 'What's tummy sticks?' followed by immediate 'I don't want to play tummy sticks!' is perfect escalation.
jokes.explanation: 'Tummy sticks' is an inspired coinage — the childish, innocent-sounding name for something clearly sexual makes it funnier than any explicit term. The beat where Jeremy asks 'What's tummy sticks?' — a moment of genuine curiosity before his survival instincts kick in — is perfect comic timing. Highly quotable and genuinely original. The invented game-name is the standout creative choice.

jokes.text: Todd: 'It's okay, I was where you were a year ago.' — said to Jeremy while being shoved into a closet
jokes.setup: Jeremy is forcibly hiding Todd in a closet
jokes.punchline: Todd offers the serene reassurance that he understands Jeremy's denial because he was 'where you were a year ago' — implying Todd was also once in denial about his sexuality
jokes.explanation: Todd's calm, knowing wisdom while literally being shoved into a closet — a perfect visual/verbal pun on 'coming out of the closet' — is brilliantly layered. The serenity of his delivery against the physical chaos is what makes it. Great character work.

jokes.text: Get in the fucking closet right now! You go get in the closet! You go get in the closet! You go get in the closet! You go get in the closet! Go!
jokes.setup: Todd refuses to hide and continues to suggest games while Jeremy spirals into panic.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's repetition of 'You go get in the closet!' five times in a row is a comedic breakdown — the panic reducing him to a skipping record.
jokes.explanation: Repetition as escalation works here primarily because of Vince Vaughn's physical delivery. As written it's weaker — the joke is in the performance more than the text. Gets a solid laugh from the unhinged energy but isn't sophisticated comedy writing.

jokes.text: I'll pop out at the right moment. / No, you will not!
jokes.setup: Jeremy has finally gotten Todd into the closet.
jokes.punchline: Todd's earnest offer to 'pop out at the right moment' — as if this is a romantic plan — and Jeremy's immediate horrified veto.
jokes.explanation: Todd's delusion that there will be a 'right moment' to reveal himself is a quick, well-executed character beat. The exchange is tight and funny. 'No, you will not!' is a perfect flat denial.

jokes.text: I was just having a bad dream. / Oh. I know about bad dreams. / You know, Todd... screams... at night sometimes. / You know, the doctors call it night terrors.
jokes.setup: Mr. Cleary has come to check on the noise. Jeremy claims he was having a bad dream. Then Todd screams from the closet.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy smoothly explains Todd's screaming from the closet as his 'night terrors' — and Mr. Cleary appears to accept this, calmly discussing his son's condition. The comedy is in the absurd normalcy of the cover story.
jokes.explanation: The comedy works on two levels: Jeremy's desperate improvisation is funny, but the bigger laugh comes from Mr. Cleary apparently believing it — suggesting this family has normalized Todd's closet-screaming behavior. The 'doctors call it night terrors' as a clinical cover for 'man hiding in closet' is well-structured irony.

jokes.text: There's nothing terrifying about the night.
jokes.setup: Mr. Cleary is leaving after the 'night terrors' explanation, having accepted it without question.
jokes.punchline: His parting reassurance — 'There's nothing terrifying about the night' — is delivered as fatherly wisdom but reads as a completely disconnected non sequitur given the actual chaos in the room.
jokes.explanation: A quiet, underplayed joke that lands because of its confident absurdity. The father's total obliviousness is the comedy — he dispenses reassurance about night terrors while his son is literally screaming in a closet. The deadpan line reads as either completely unaware or deeply repressed. Either reading is funny.

jokes.text: Jeremy negotiating with Todd to go to sleep: 'If I get my sleep I'll have to... I'll... I'll love to make time and talk about, uh, uh, different things. Like paintings.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy is desperately trying to get Todd to leave him alone for the night
jokes.punchline: His hasty promise to discuss 'different things — like paintings' inadvertently plays into Todd's artistic romantic gesture (the painting called 'Celebration')
jokes.explanation: The accidental callback to the painting is funny — Jeremy is trying to placate Todd without realizing he's playing directly into Todd's romantic narrative. Solid character-based comedy.

jokes.text: Mmm. Okay. That was nice. That was nice! Please let me just sleep.
jokes.setup: After the night terrors crisis passes, Jeremy is trying to get Todd out of his room and go to sleep.
jokes.punchline: The 'That was nice. That was nice!' paired with 'Please let me just sleep' implies Todd has done something to Jeremy (a kiss, a touch) that Jeremy can't bring himself to fully reject but is desperately negotiating around.
jokes.explanation: The ambiguity of 'that was nice' is the joke — Jeremy is diplomatically managing an unwanted advance without fully condemning it, which is funnier than outright rejection. The exhausted desperation in 'Please let me just sleep' sells the cringe.

jokes.text: I can't take this fuckin' shit anymore!
jokes.setup: The entire sequence of nocturnal tortures — Gloria, Todd, the painting, tummy sticks — has accumulated to a breaking point.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's final explosion after the long suppressed cringe sequence is the cumulative punchline to everything that's happened since 66:31.
jokes.explanation: As a line of dialogue it's not creative, but as a structural beat it's effective — it functions as a release valve for accumulated cringe tension. The impact comes from the buildup, not the words themselves.

jokes.text: Or, it could've been the midnight rape... or the nude, gay art show that took place in my room... one of those probably added to the lack of sleep.
jokes.setup: John asks why Jeremy looks tired. Jeremy sarcastically suggests it could have been the 'soft mattress.'
jokes.punchline: Jeremy escalates from 'soft mattress' to 'midnight rape' and 'nude, gay art show' — cataloguing his night with the vocabulary of an insurance claim.
jokes.explanation: The comedy comes from the forced neutrality of the delivery — these are presented as a clinical list of inconveniences alongside 'soft mattress.' 'Nude, gay art show' as a summary of the Todd painting incident is a perfect compression. High quotability and strong callback structure. The escalation from domestic complaint to assault is sharp.

jokes.text: Try one of these scones, you're gonna love 'em.
jokes.setup: Jeremy has just described being raped and subjected to a nude gay art show.
jokes.punchline: John's response is to recommend the scones. The complete non-acknowledgment of the horror Jeremy described — pivoting immediately to brunch enthusiasm — is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic indifference. John's complete absorption in the breakfast buffet while his friend describes a sexual assault is both a character moment and a sharp timing gag. The economy is near-perfect — five words do enormous comedic work by their context. It's a great 'straight man enthusiastically ignoring the crisis' beat.

jokes.text: I'm a little traumatized to have a scone.
jokes.setup: John recommends the scones despite Jeremy's traumatic night.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's response that he's 'a little traumatized to have a scone' is a masterful understatement — 'a little traumatized' doing heavy lifting.
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of 'traumatized' and 'scone' is very funny. The word 'scone' is inherently a little comic (too genteel), and placing trauma next to it creates a perfect deflation. The delivery of 'a little' as qualifier makes it funnier still — trauma so significant he can't eat a baked good, described with British-tea-party vocabulary.

jokes.text: John: 'The whole eyedrop thing backfired. Okay? It didn't work. She had to leave me and go attend to him.'
jokes.setup: John's scheme to make Sack sick with eyedrops (established in earlier reels) was supposed to give him time with Claire
jokes.punchline: The plan backfired — it made Sack sick enough that Claire had to attend to him, actually reducing John's access to her
jokes.explanation: A plot beat more than a comedy beat, but the ironic backfire of a scheme is a standard comedic structure. Functional but not particularly inventive.

jokes.text: I just had my own sock duct-taped into my mouth last night! ... the sock that I wore around all day, playin' football in, pouring sweat in, was shoved into my mouth, and there was duct tape over it!
jokes.setup: John is trying to get Jeremy to stay at the estate to help his pursuit of Claire. Jeremy is listing reasons he must leave.
jokes.punchline: The duct-taped sock revelation — with the increasingly specific and revolting detail ('played football in, pouring sweat in') — is a callback to the overnight horrors, now with new information that makes everything worse.
jokes.explanation: The escalating specificity is what makes this exceptional — 'playing football in, pouring sweat in' transforms the horror from abstract to viscerally physical. Each additional detail gets worse. The audience's imagination does the work once the image is planted. Strong rewatch bonus because the detail rewards attention. High quotability.

jokes.text: Well, let's talk about it. I'm a good listener.
jokes.setup: Jeremy has just described being gagged with his own sweat-soaked sock.
jokes.punchline: John's completely calm therapeutic response — 'let's talk about it, I'm a good listener' — ignores the severity of the situation in favor of his own romantic agenda.
jokes.explanation: Another beat of John's selfish cheerfulness as a comedic device. Works but is a variation on the same joke as the scone line — slightly less fresh for coming second.

jokes.text: I felt like Jodie Foster in 'The Accused' last night.
jokes.setup: Jeremy is describing the horrific nature of his night.
jokes.punchline: Comparing his experience to Jodie Foster's gang-rape in 'The Accused' — a notoriously harrowing film — is a dark, transgressive pop culture reference that lands because it's both absurdly over-the-top and oddly apt.
jokes.explanation: Dark pop culture reference with genuine punch. The specificity of the film title rather than a generic rape-movie reference is what elevates it. Character-specific: only Jeremy would escalate to this comparison. The reference does require cultural knowledge, slightly limiting mass impact.

jokes.text: I'm gonna go home, see Dr. Finkelstein and I'm gonna tell him... we got a whole new bag of issues, we can forget about Mom for a while.
jokes.setup: Jeremy announces he's leaving and going home.
jokes.punchline: The therapy reference — telling his therapist they have 'a whole new bag of issues' and can 'forget about Mom for a while' — is a funny character detail implying Jeremy has been in therapy for mother issues, which are now eclipsed.
jokes.explanation: A quick, funny character detail that expands Jeremy's backstory economically. 'Forget about Mom for a while' implies years of therapy undone by one weekend. Good character integration.

jokes.text: A friend in need is a pest.
jokes.setup: John has invoked 'Rule #1: Never leave a fellow crasher behind' and guilted Jeremy about being selfish. Jeremy concedes to staying.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy inverts the proverb 'a friend in need is a friend indeed' into 'a friend in need is a pest' — a perfectly sour summary of his capitulation.
jokes.explanation: A line that earns its 8.0 craft score. The proverb inversion is structurally perfect — it uses a well-known phrase and flips exactly one word to devastating effect. 'Pest' is the precisely right word: not 'enemy,' not 'burden,' but pest — implying Jeremy's affection is real but his annoyance is genuine too. Highly quotable, economical, and character-specific. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in its precision and memorability.

jokes.text: I'll stick it out with you because you're desperate. I need you. I'm gonna try to give you a little bit more time, because somebody can't close.
jokes.setup: Jeremy reluctantly agrees to stay and help John, framing it as an act of generosity.
jokes.punchline: 'Somebody can't close' — Jeremy's characterization of John's romantic failure using sales/pickup terminology — is the sharp edge. The whole exchange is a comedy of wounded male ego.
jokes.explanation: Functional character-comedy banter. 'Can't close' is a good line in context. The scene works more as character establishment than as pure comedy.

jokes.text: Jeremy: 'I'm gonna try to give you a little bit more time, because somebody can't close.'
jokes.setup: Jeremy is agreeing to stay but needs to establish dominance in the negotiation
jokes.punchline: 'Because somebody can't close' — a sales/crasher-world term applied to John's romantic fumbling, delivered with mock condescension
jokes.explanation: The 'close' terminology from their wedding-crashing world applied to John's genuine romantic situation creates a funny friction — John has stopped treating this as a game and Jeremy still is.

jokes.text: Number one: Stop being a pussy. Number two: Make a move. Number three... you know it.
jokes.setup: Jeremy agrees to give John 'a little more time' and offers his conditions and advice.
jokes.punchline: The 'Number three... you know it' — implying a third rule so obvious it doesn't need stating — is funnier than any explicit third rule would be. The audience fills it in as something crude.
jokes.explanation: The elliptical 'you know it' is a good piece of implied comedy — the unspoken rule is funnier because it's not said. Good economy.

jokes.text: Could you pop the syrup for me? Just as a top off? / Here's what's gonna happen, Tonto. Kimosabe's gonna have some flavor...
jokes.setup: In the middle of delivering tough-love rules advice, Jeremy makes an elaborate point about breakfast etiquette.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's refusal to share the dining experience with John — 'I like to recharge my batteries, and shut down the engines, and get myself back to neutral' — framed with the Lone Ranger reference ('Tonto,' 'Kimosabe') is an absurd elevation of breakfast privacy.
jokes.explanation: Jeremy's food/personal-space rituals are a consistent character note. The Lone Ranger framing is an odd but funny choice. 'Kimosabe's gonna have some flavor' is a good line. The scene runs slightly long but the bits within it work.

jokes.text: Can I tell you something without you getting angry? / I love you. Yeah, you, big guy. / I love you too.
jokes.setup: John has an earnest question for Jeremy. The audience anticipates some practical tactical advice.
jokes.punchline: John says 'I love you' to Jeremy — sincerely. After a beat, Jeremy returns it. It's the punchline to the whole contentious negotiation: underneath their bickering these two genuinely love each other.
jokes.explanation: A warm misdirection that earns its laugh through sincerity. The comic setup — 'can I tell you something without you getting angry' — primes the audience for a complaint; the pivot to 'I love you' is unexpected and lands as both funny and genuine.
