Character integration is strong: this is exactly who these two men are. Rewatch bonus because it recontextualizes the whole argument.

jokes.text: Oh, it was boring, you know, but the bachelor party, of course, rocked. We got Heidi a couple of those fucking sluts from the environmental group...
jokes.setup: Sack calls a friend and gives his review of the weekend's events.
jokes.punchline: The characterization of women at an environmental group as 'fucking sluts' available for sexual use — presented as casual boasting — is a pure villain-reveal moment. The comedy is in the awfulness.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that this is precisely what we'd expect from Sack — the dialogue perfectly crystallizes his villainy. The comedy is character-based cringe rather than wit. The awfulness is the point; it makes us root for John.

jokes.text: Sack: 'She's saving the world one maladjusted kid at a time. But that'll all change when we're married, 'cause I want a wife. I don't want a fucking martyr, right?'
jokes.setup: Sack is describing Claire's work to his friend on the phone
jokes.punchline: His framing of Claire's work as martyrdom that he plans to end when married — delivered with casual certainty — is darkly funny in how it reveals the full extent of his awfulness
jokes.explanation: 'I don't want a fucking martyr' is a funny specific choice of word — his contempt for her idealism is efficiently conveyed. It's a villain establishing his villainy but done with enough wit to be genuinely funny.

jokes.text: She's saving the world one maladjusted kid at a time. But that'll all change when we're married, 'cause I want a wife. I don't want a fucking martyr, right?
jokes.setup: Sack is asked about Claire and her life choices.
jokes.punchline: 'I don't want a fucking martyr' — Sack's framing of Claire's social work as a problem to be corrected post-marriage — is both a funny line and a devastating character indictment.
jokes.explanation: 'Saving the world one maladjusted kid at a time' is a genuinely clever turn of phrase — it's how an awful person summarizes noble work. 'I don't want a fucking martyr' is quotable. The sequence works as character comedy that also advances the plot: we now fully understand why Claire might be scared.

jokes.text: Mr. Cleary re Sack: 'Well then, "The Woodwind" takes off without him.'
jokes.setup: Sack is apparently still sick; Claire reports this
jokes.punchline: Cleary's flat, unapologetic decision to leave Sack behind — no negotiation, no sympathy — reveals his authority and mild contempt for Sack even as a future son-in-law
jokes.explanation: Good deadpan authority moment for Cleary. The naming of the boat 'The Woodwind' is a funny detail and his dismissal of Sack is characterful.

jokes.text: You know, I'm used to sailing down under with the Kiwis, so everything is backwards. Even the toilets... when you flush them, the water spins the opposite way. Really freaks you out the first time you see it.
jokes.setup: John has just demonstrated total incompetence at sailing (pointing starboard the wrong way). He needs to explain away his mistake.
jokes.punchline: John's cover story — that he usually sails 'down under with the Kiwis' so everything is backwards, including the toilets — is an absurd non sequitur excuse. The toilet detail is the tell: it's the flourish of a con man who oversells the lie.
jokes.explanation: The toilet detail is brilliant character writing — a skilled liar knows to add a vivid, specific, irrelevant detail to make a story believable. John doesn't just claim to sail differently; he provides an unasked-for corroborating detail about toilet water direction. The audience understands this is a con in action. High character integration because only John — a practiced social chameleon — would instinctively do this.

jokes.text: John: 'You know, I'm used to sailing down under with the Kiwis, so everything is backwards. Even the toilets... when you flush them, the water spins the opposite way. Really freaks you out the first time you see it.'
jokes.setup: John has just been caught not knowing starboard; he needs to recover
jokes.punchline: His cover story — 'sailing down under with the Kiwis' — where everything is 'backwards,' pivoting weirdly to toilet flush direction as his explanation, is a delightfully absurd save
jokes.explanation: John's desperate pivot to toilets to explain his nautical error is an inspired bullshitter's move — it's confident, specific, and completely irrelevant to the actual error. The toilet detail is funny because it's true (the Coriolis effect myth) and yet has nothing to do with knowing starboard. Great con-man character work.

jokes.text: Mr. Environmental is also a hunter. It's kind of an interesting combination. / I hunt quail, Jeremy! They're overpopulated in this region and they're decimating the grub worm population. You got a fucking problem with that?!
jokes.setup: Jeremy makes a mild, slightly smug observation about Sack being both an environmentalist and a hunter.
jokes.punchline: Sack's immediate explosive defense — with the specific ecological justification ('decimating the grub worm population') delivered at attack volume — is a perfect character explosion. The specificity of 'grub worm' is the detail that makes it.
jokes.explanation: The comic engine here is Sack's hair-trigger defensiveness deployed against a mild-mannered observation. The ecological rationalization — clearly rehearsed and immediately weaponized — reveals Sack's pathology perfectly. 'Grub worm population' is the perfect absurd specific. High character integration.

jokes.text: Not nearly as much as I do with the, uh, attire that you have on, or just your general point of view towards everybody. But let's go kill some birds. I'm psyched.
jokes.setup: Sack has just aggressively challenged Jeremy about whether he has a problem with quail hunting.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's response first admits to problems with Sack's outfit and 'general point of view' — a comprehensive dismissal of the man's entire being — then pivots to cheerful compliance: 'let's go kill some birds. I'm psyched.'
jokes.explanation: A bravura line. 'Your general point of view towards everybody' is a comprehensive insult dressed as a mild concern. The pivot to 'let's go kill some birds. I'm psyched' — delivered with complete sincerity — is a perfect tonal whiplash. The 'I'm psyched' is the topper that sells it. This is Vince Vaughn's character at his comic best: aggressive politeness masking real aggression.

jokes.text: The whole 17 years we've known each other, I've been sneaking off to go on little hunting trips around the world. / No, I don't even know what the fuck a quail is!
jokes.setup: John asks if Jeremy has shot a gun before, apparently expecting some competence.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's confident opener — 17 years of secret hunting trips — immediately collapses: 'No, I don't even know what the fuck a quail is.' The setup of expertise followed by zero knowledge is the comic structure.
jokes.explanation: A clean setup/punchline with good structure — the 17-year buildup exists entirely to detonate with 'I don't even know what the fuck a quail is.' The setup is longer than necessary, but the punchline earns it. Character-specific: Jeremy's bravado masking total cluelessness is core to who he is.

jokes.text: I feel totally ridiculous. Like why do I have to be in camouflage? So the big bad quail doesn't see me?
jokes.setup: Jeremy and John are dressed in hunting camouflage for a quail hunt.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's observation — why wear camouflage to hunt a small ground bird — is an actually reasonable question asked with mock-defensive indignation that makes it funny.
jokes.explanation: 'The big bad quail' is the punchline within the punchline — the absurdity of treating a quail as a threatening adversary. Good observational comedy with a slight absurdist edge.

jokes.text: I know. It's like, why can't we hunt something cool like a hawk, or an eagle, or something with some talons? ... Or a fucking human being? That'll get you jacked up.
jokes.setup: John and Jeremy are commiserating about the indignity of quail hunting.
jokes.punchline: The escalation from hawks to eagles to gorillas to rhinoceros to 'a fucking human being' — The Most Dangerous Game reference — is a perfectly structured absurdist escalation that goes dark fast.
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure is clean and well-paced. 'Something with some talons' is a funny specific. The pivot to hunting humans lands as dark comedy. 'Get you jacked up' is an odd choice of phrase that's funnier than it should be. The scene runs slightly long but the escalation earns it.

jokes.text: I mean, like... you're hunting a human being right now, the most dangerous game. Like a worthy adversary. Not a human being that's armed... but a clever... a clever human being who knows the jungle, or the woods. Or like a bad guy.
jokes.setup: John has suggested hunting a human being. Jeremy takes this seriously and begins to refine the parameters.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's earnest elaboration on the ideal human-hunting scenario — 'not a human being that's armed... but a clever human being who knows the jungle' — building to the deflating 'or like a bad guy,' treats a psychotic proposal as a reasonable sporting discussion.
jokes.explanation: 'Or like a bad guy' is the perfect landing after the elaborate moral framework — it deflates the whole construction. The earnestness with which Jeremy constructs rules for murdering humans is the comedic engine. Slightly long in delivery.

jokes.text: Jeremy gets shot / 'They got me!' reaction
jokes.setup: Sack has orchestrated a 'hunting accident' to shoot at John and Jeremy. A shot rings out.
jokes.punchline: Jeremy gets hit — his 'They got me!' reaction, a melodramatic take on being pelted with what is probably birdshot, plays as slapstick action-movie parody.
jokes.explanation: A physical comedy moment that works more through execution (Vince Vaughn's physical performance implied) than writing. 'They got me!' is a fun genre-parody reaction. Functional slapstick.

jokes.text: Oh, don't 'okay, buddy' me. Look, we just came by to say we're gonna take a little bike ride and then we're gonna come back and check up on you. / I hope you flip your bike over and knock your two front teeth out, you selfish son of a bitch! You leave me in the trenches taking grenades, John!
jokes.setup: John tries to be sympathetic to the shot Jeremy while also escaping to spend time with Claire. Jeremy is furious.
jokes.punchline: 'I hope you flip your bike over and knock your two front teeth out' is a perfectly specific and oddly domestic curse. 'You leave me in the trenches taking grenades' — metaphorizing the Todd/Gloria situation as actual warfare — is the funniest line in this exchange.
jokes.explanation: 'Taking grenades' is a genuinely great metaphor for absorbing unwanted sexual attention so your wingman can pursue his target — it reframes the entire running gag with military vocabulary that makes Jeremy's sacrifice both funny and oddly heroic. 'You leave me in the trenches taking grenades, John!' is a highly quotable line that became part of the film's cultural footprint. 'Flip your bike over and knock your two front teeth out' is delightfully specific in its pettiness.

jokes.text: John's venture capitalist monologue about going down a road and not intending the life you're living
jokes.setup: Claire asks John about his work as a 'venture capitalist' (a fake identity).
jokes.punchline: John delivers a speech about not intending the life you end up living — 'you get caught up in it and you're kind of into it and just don't even have time to really ask questions about it' — which is nakedly a description of his own fraudulent wedding-crashing lifestyle. Claire takes it as sincere vulnerability.
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony is the joke — John is accidentally telling the truth while lying. The audience sees both levels simultaneously. It's a smarter piece of comedy than it might appear: the character uses his real feelings about his life as a prop in a con, and doesn't realize it. Strong rewatch bonus because knowing the truth makes every word funnier.

jokes.text: Well... you're not that young.
jokes.setup: John has said 'I'm still young' in response to questions about his unrealized potential and life plans.
jokes.punchline: Claire's dry, honest correction — 'you're not that young' — lands as an unexpected bit of bluntness that punctures the romantic reverie.
jokes.explanation: Four words that earn a genuine laugh through perfect economy and timing. The directness is unexpected in a flirtatious scene and reveals Claire's character: she's not going to indulge easy self-flattery. 'Not that young' is careful phrasing — not 'you're old,' which would be cruel, but a precise calibration. Well-executed deadpan.

jokes.text: Claire: 'Well... you're not that young.' — in response to John saying 'I'm still young'
jokes.setup: John has been musing philosophically about unfulfilled potential and says 'We'll see. I'm still young.'
jokes.punchline: Claire's immediate, slightly apologetic correction — 'Well... you're not that young' — delivered with a beat and then 'I'm sorry' is a perfect deadpan deflation
jokes.explanation: The 'you're not that young' + 'I'm sorry' combination is excellently timed — the apology implies she meant to think it but it slipped out, which is funnier than a deliberate insult. The ellipsis beat before 'you're not that young' is crucial. Great economy.

jokes.text: Do you want it full speed or half speed? / Full. / You're never gonna hit me, I don't think. I'm pretty quick.
jokes.setup: Claire and John play a hand-slapping game (a physical trust/speed game). Claire offers half speed as an option.
jokes.punchline: John chooses full speed and immediately loses, as Claire's confident 'you're never gonna hit me, I don't think. I'm pretty quick' establishes her as the dominant one in this physical competition — reversing expected gender dynamics.
jokes.explanation: A light flirtatious game that's charming rather than hilarious. Claire's quiet confidence is a good character note. The comedy is mild — it's more of a rom-com grace note than a joke.

jokes.text: No, because you're supposed to... You gotta wait until I put them back! / Come on!
jokes.setup: John has apparently slapped Claire's hands before she was ready in the hand-slap game.
jokes.punchline: His protests about the rules — 'you gotta wait until I put them back!' — while she laughs suggests he cheated/flinched and is now complaining. The reversal of John being outmaneuvered by Claire in a simple game is the comedy.
jokes.explanation: Light physical comedy that works in context as a flirtatious moment. As a joke in isolation it's thin — the comedy is primarily in the actors' physical interaction rather than anything in the writing.

jokes.text: That's my rationalization and I'm sticking to it. / Fair enough. / And I don't mean to pry. / Yes you do.
jokes.setup: Claire is rationalizing her fear about marrying Sack, admitting 'I think that's how everyone feels before they're about to get married, don't you think?' Then catches herself.
jokes.punchline: Claire's self-aware 'That's my rationalization and I'm sticking to it' is good; John's 'Yes you do' — a flat refutation of her 'I don't mean to pry' — is the sharper joke. It's honest and slightly cheeky.
jokes.explanation: 'Yes you do' is a perfectly economical character moment — John sees through Claire's polite self-deprecation and calls it, which is both bold and intimate. 'That's my rationalization and I'm sticking to it' is an appealingly self-aware line. The exchange works as rom-com wit.

jokes.text: Claire: 'But I think that that's how everyone feels before they're about to get married. I mean, don't you think? Yeah, no. Don't answer that. That's my rationalization and I'm sticking to it.'
jokes.setup: Claire is confessing fear about marrying Sack and reaching for a universal truth to validate it
jokes.punchline: She immediately instructs John not to answer her rhetorical question — 'Don't answer that' — aware her rationalization needs protecting from scrutiny
jokes.explanation: 'That's my rationalization and I'm sticking to it' is a genuinely good line — self-aware about the irrationality but committed anyway. The structure of asking a question and then immediately withdrawing it is psychologically true and funny.

jokes.text: Sack announces his engagement to Claire just as John has declared he's in love with her — reaction beat as John realizes he's lost
jokes.setup: John has just confessed to Jeremy that he thinks he's in love with Claire and plans to tell her the truth
jokes.punchline: Before he can act, Sack publicly announces their engagement in front of the whole family, perfectly timing John's worst possible moment
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant — the engagement announcement lands as a comedic gut-punch because the audience just heard John declare his love. The irony is clean and well-timed. The rewatch bonus comes from knowing exactly how much John's stomach must drop.

jokes.text: Jeremy's speech about Gloria's virginity being special — "Oh, I wasn't a virgin. Far from it. I just thought that's what guys wanted to hear."
jokes.setup: Jeremy is patronizingly explaining to Gloria that she only has strong feelings for him because he was her first — building up to let her down gently with false tenderness
jokes.punchline: Gloria casually punctures his entire ego-driven narrative: she was never a virgin and simply told him what she thought he wanted to hear
jokes.explanation: This is one of the best jokes in the reel. The setup lets Jeremy monologue from a position of total false superiority, and the punchline demolishes him on every level simultaneously — the virginity, the mystical significance he attached to it, and his self-image as the experienced seducer. 'Far from it' is perfect economy. Character-specific: only Gloria's particular brand of manipulative practicality makes this land exactly this way.

jokes.text: Jeremy's stunned reaction — wide-eyed silence / "Come on. Jeremy!" — after learning Gloria was never a virgin
jokes.setup: Gloria has just revealed she fabricated the virginity story
jokes.punchline: Jeremy is so shattered he is literally speechless — a massive comedic pause before he runs/stumbles off (inferred from "Jeremy!" being called after him)
jokes.explanation: Vince Vaughn's physical performance is implied to be enormous here — the stunned 'Wow!' and then fleeing while Gloria calls after him. Gets a big laugh primarily off the back of joke #3, which makes it a dependent beat rather than a standalone joke.

jokes.text: "Can I ask you a question, Father? Do you ever get horny?"
jokes.setup: Jeremy is at a low point, sitting with a Catholic priest who is offering him the sacrament and comfort
jokes.punchline: Jeremy, in full emotional spiral, pivots immediately to asking the priest about his sex drive
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeremy — his version of a sincere heart-to-heart is to ask a celibate priest about erections. The collision between sacred setting and Jeremy's relentlessly sexual worldview is a strong character joke. The delivery is Vaughn's specialty: sincere tone, insane content.

jokes.text: "Does that get tough sometimes? You ever pull on yourself, or... No. Everything works? Do you get swelled up still? Yeah, of course. Well, what do you do? You pray. Yeah, I pray, too, you know what I mean?"
jokes.setup: Jeremy has asked the priest if he gets horny — the priest is politely deflecting
jokes.punchline: Jeremy escalates through increasingly explicit questions about priestly celibacy, finally equating prayer with masturbation
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'do you get horny' to 'do you get swelled up' to the priest calmly saying 'you pray' and Jeremy treating that as relatable is a beautiful three-beat structure. The priest's monosyllabic responses against Jeremy's verbal avalanche is excellent comic contrast. The final 'Yeah, I pray too' equating sexual frustration with prayer lands as the peak.

jokes.text: "I had an imaginary friend when I was a kid. His name was Shilo! We used to play checkers with each other every day, and bless his heart, Shilo'd always let me win!"
jokes.setup: Jeremy is arguing that his attraction to crazy Gloria proves he has a hidden wild side
jokes.punchline: His evidence: an imaginary friend named Shilo who let him win at checkers — delivered as though this proves he's a dangerous eccentric
jokes.explanation: This is the standout line of the priest sequence. The specificity of 'his name was Shilo' and 'bless his heart, Shilo'd always let me win' is what elevates it from an absurdist throwaway to something genuinely memorable. It perfectly captures Jeremy's oblivious self-mythology — he thinks this proves he's a little crazy, while the audience hears a completely normal and slightly sad childhood anecdote. The gap between his self-perception and reality IS the joke, and it's delivered with beautiful earnestness.

jokes.text: 'And that ain't normal! There's something odd in that...' — delivered with utter sincerity as Jeremy's most self-aware moment
jokes.setup: Jeremy has just told the priest about Shilo the imaginary checkers friend.
jokes.punchline: He pauses to acknowledge 'that ain't normal' — but the understatement is that the ENTIRE conversation has been wildly abnormal; he's only now noticing one specific detail.
jokes.explanation: A button that works because of the gap between what Jeremy considers abnormal (the imaginary friend) and what the audience knows is abnormal (literally everything Jeremy has said for the past minute). Solid but not special.

jokes.text: Jeremy hugs the priest and says "I love ya. You're a sweet man." — Priest's reaction: "Oh, dear God."
jokes.setup: Jeremy has just delivered a 90-second emotional monologue to a stranger priest about masturbation, insanity, and his imaginary friend
jokes.punchline: He wraps it up by going in for a physical embrace and declaring love; the priest's response is a quiet, devastated prayer
jokes.explanation: 'Oh, dear God' from a priest in this context is a small gem — perfectly economical capper. The priest literally praying in distress after this experience is the priest's one joke in the whole exchange and it lands clean.

jokes.text: John tells Claire "You can't marry this guy" and "Because I've fallen for you" — immediately followed by "Oh, good news travels fast"
jokes.setup: John has pulled Claire aside for his heartfelt confession at her engagement party
jokes.punchline: Before he can even get through the declaration, someone else walks over — implying the whole party already knows he's making a scene. 'Good news travels fast' is the dry deflation.
jokes.explanation: Functional interruption gag. The timing is sharp but the line itself is not remarkable. Works as a beat in a larger sequence.

jokes.text: "Trapster, talk to me. No shit."
jokes.setup: Sack is apparently getting a Secret Service/security briefing about John being on the property
jokes.punchline: His nickname for his security contact ('Trapster') and his terse 'No shit' response suggests his paranoid security apparatus is an absurd overkill for a beach engagement party
jokes.explanation: Mildly amusing character bit. 'Trapster' is a nice comic detail — Sack has a thug nickname for his guy — but the joke doesn't go anywhere particularly surprising.

jokes.text: John tells Claire he's fallen for her; she says 'Maybe'; he responds 'Maybe. That's all I needed to know' — then immediately starts his confession about being a wedding crasher
jokes.setup: John gets the tentative romantic acknowledgment he's been building toward — 'Maybe' — and treats it as full vindication
jokes.punchline: He then immediately pivots to 'I need to talk to you about that... you might want to sit back on the swing' — suggesting his confession is so bad it requires seating
jokes.explanation: The 'you might want to sit down' beat is a classic stall that works here because we know exactly how bad what's coming is. Functional setup for the revelation sequence.

jokes.text: "Run! Johnny! She's trying to kill me! Grandma! Whoa whoa! Get the gun from her! Put the gun down! This is the real world, lady! You can't just go shooting people on a whim!"
jokes.setup: Jeremy apparently told Gloria's grandmother something in private, and she's now chasing him with a gun
jokes.punchline: The chaos erupts with 'She's trying to kill me!' and the absurdist scolding 'You can't just go shooting people on a whim!' — which is both true and a hilariously inadequate response to a gun
jokes.explanation: 'You can't just go shooting people on a whim' is the standout line here — it's both literally correct and comically insufficient as a response to active gun violence. The slapstick chaos lands as broad physical comedy.

jokes.text: "What did you do? I told you that in confidence! That was a confession! What are you talking about?"
jokes.setup: The priest apparently revealed Jeremy's confessed secrets to the family, causing the chaos
jokes.punchline: Jeremy invokes the sanctity of the confessional — which is funny because his 'confession' to the priest was an unsolicited rant about his sex life, not a formal sacrament
jokes.explanation: Solid callback that retroactively recontextualizes the priest scene. Jeremy treating his unsolicited oversharing as legally protected confession is a good character-specific joke. The priest betraying confessional confidence is an added layer of absurdity.

jokes.text: "Yes... with shades of grey."
jokes.setup: Claire demands a yes or no answer on whether John crashed their family's wedding to sleep with women
jokes.punchline: John, after a beat, admits 'Yes' — but then adds '...with shades of grey' as though that nuances a yes/no question
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the reel. The structure is perfect: Claire builds tension with 'yes or no?' repeated twice, John takes a full beat, says the damning 'Yes' — and then the deflation of '...with shades of grey' is both cowardly and completely in character. It's the most economical possible way to both admit guilt and refuse responsibility. Highly quotable precisely because it captures a universal human impulse to hedge on an unanswerable question.

jokes.text: "I'm not perfect, but who are we kidding? Neither are you."
jokes.setup: John has just admitted he crashed the wedding under a fake identity
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots to 'but you're not perfect either' as a defense — an astonishing piece of whataboutism from a man who has just been completely exposed
jokes.explanation: Good character joke — John's self-serving audacity in turning his admission into a mutual criticism is both enraging and funny. Works as a character beat more than a pure laugh line.

jokes.text: "And you wanna know what? I dig it!" — Jeremy's voice echoing as his and Gloria's parallel confession implodes
jokes.setup: Jeremy told Claire's family he 'digs' Gloria's craziness during his priest monologue
jokes.punchline: The same phrase 'I dig it!' is now blurted out in the middle of the chaotic family meltdown, suggesting Jeremy's enthusiasm has not diminished despite the gun
jokes.explanation: Modest callback. 'I dig it' reappearing in chaos is a nice structural echo but doesn't add much new information or surprise.

jokes.text: "Jeremy tried to seduce me!" — Todd (the gay brother) pipes up in the middle of the family crisis
jokes.setup: The family confrontation is about John and Jeremy's fraudulent identities as wedding crashers
jokes.punchline: Todd introduces a completely separate grievance mid-crisis: Jeremy apparently led him on romantically
jokes.explanation: Perfectly timed comedic interruption. The chaos is about wedding-crashing, and Todd uses it to surface his entirely personal romantic complaint. It's character-specific (only Todd would do this) and the timing in the middle of a gun-and-family meltdown makes it land hard.

jokes.text: "You did?" — Jeremy's surprised reaction to Todd's accusation
jokes.setup: Todd accuses Jeremy of trying to seduce him
jokes.punchline: John, in the middle of his own disaster, still takes a moment to turn to Jeremy with genuine 'You did?' — equal parts accusatory and impressed
jokes.explanation: Two words that do a lot of work. John's ability to be simultaneously devastated and curious about Jeremy's Todd situation in this moment is very funny. Economy is nearly perfect.

jokes.text: "I want my painting back. The painting was a gift, Todd. I'm taking it with me."
jokes.setup: Todd accused Jeremy of seduction; the family confrontation is spiraling
jokes.punchline: Todd's response to the entire crisis is to demand his painting back — a petty, domestic complaint in the middle of an explosive family reckoning
jokes.explanation: The painting dispute as the final indignity of the confrontation is a nice comic beat. Jeremy treating the painting as his rightful property ('it was a gift') while Todd is emotionally invested is a small but well-drawn character clash.

jokes.text: "You had me going, son. I thought it was something special." — Secretary Cleary delivering his quiet, disappointed send-off
jokes.setup: John has been exposed as a fake who crashed the family's wedding
jokes.punchline: The Secretary of the Treasury delivers a dignified, almost fatherly disappointment rather than outrage — 'You had me going, son' — as though John was a promising intern who embezzled
jokes.explanation: Christopher Walken's particular energy makes 'You had me going, son' funnier than it reads on paper. The measured, presidential disappointment rather than anger is a consistent character note that plays well here.

jokes.text: "Now bunch those panties up into a little ball. Put that little ball right in your mouth."
jokes.setup: The audience cuts to Jeremy months later — apparently recovered from the Gloria crisis — in the middle of a phone call that is clearly sexual in nature
jokes.punchline: He's on the phone with a woman, delivering what are clearly phone-sex instructions, before being interrupted by John walking in
jokes.explanation: The reintroduction of Jeremy post-time-skip — and he's exactly the same — is good character economy. 'Bunch those panties into a little ball' is specific enough to be funny on its own. The transition is brisk and immediately characterizing.

jokes.text: "What the fuck? You can't knock anymore?"
jokes.setup: John has just walked in on Jeremy mid-phone-sex call (or whatever the Larry call was)
jokes.punchline: Jeremy's response is not embarrassment but indignation — as if walking in on this is John's social failure, not his
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat — Jeremy's shamelessness is the joke. The line itself is not remarkable but it maintains his consistent characterization.

jokes.text: Jeremy's list of John's failed romantic attempts: letters, phone calls, candygram, and 'the little kitten that you got her' — 'Because she didn't keep it and I know you're not raising that goddamn thing'
jokes.setup: Jeremy is trying to convince John that Claire has moved on, listing all the outreach attempts she's ignored
jokes.punchline: The escalating list climaxes with the kitten — and Jeremy's parenthetical panic about where the kitten IS NOW implies John may have adopted a cat he doesn't want
jokes.explanation: The kitten is the perfect comedic escalation of John's romantic desperation. 'God knows what happened to that little kitten' followed by 'I know you're not raising that goddamn thing' is a great joke about the unintended consequences of grand romantic gestures. The kitten is a perfect absurd detail — sending a live animal as a romantic overture.

jokes.text: John calls Jeremy 'Tasmanian devil' mid-argument
jokes.setup: John is trying to convince Jeremy to go to the engagement party with him.
jokes.punchline: 'Okay okay, listen to me, Tasmanian devil.' — an affectionate insult nickname deployed to disarm Jeremy's objections.
jokes.explanation: Quick nickname gag — 'Tasmanian devil' fits Jeremy's energy perfectly but doesn't do much more than describe him. Functional comic texture.

jokes.text: "What is your deal? What is your problem? For the past couple of months you've been a ghost... I thrive on enthusiasm. Don't take the wind out of my sails. I need you."
jokes.setup: Jeremy reasonably points out there will be Secret Service and they have no chance of getting in
jokes.punchline: John dismisses the legitimate security objection with 'your goddamn negativity' and 'I thrive on enthusiasm' — framing reasonable caution as a personal betrayal
jokes.explanation: 'I thrive on enthusiasm' is a good line — John is essentially accusing Jeremy of being a buzzkill for raising the objection that there will be Secret Service agents with their photos. The gap between the legitimate concern and John's inspirational-speaker reframe is funny.

jokes.text: "I'm two steps ahead of you and 10 steps ahead of Secret Service."
jokes.setup: Jeremy says they can't possibly crash a party with Secret Service who have pictures of them
jokes.punchline: John responds with total unearned confidence: he is TEN STEPS ahead of professional government security
jokes.explanation: Classic overconfidence joke. The specific '10 steps ahead of Secret Service' is funny because it's such an absurd claim, and because we know his plan will be waiter costumes.

jokes.text: "Oh, yeah. 46 extra long, baba ganoush special. We're waiters!"
jokes.setup: John has claimed to be 10 steps ahead of Secret Service with his master plan
jokes.punchline: The grand plan is revealed: they're wearing waiter uniforms. The 'baba ganoush special' is apparently a sizing nickname for an oversized waiter jacket — the deflation from 'masterplan' to 'we bought some uniforms' is the joke
jokes.explanation: 'Baba ganoush special' is a funny piece of absurdist specificity — it sounds like something a costume rental shop worker would actually say. The comedic payoff of the '10-steps-ahead master plan' being waiter costumes works through classic expectation deflation.

jokes.text: "Buddy, for your own good, you gotta let this thing go. Now, I'm gonna meet you there at 7:30, okay?"
jokes.setup: Jeremy spends 30 seconds insisting he will absolutely not go to this party — it's crazy, it's impossible, he won't do it
jokes.punchline: He immediately capitulates and gives John a meetup time, as if he had agreed all along
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom reversal — the character argues emphatically against something and then immediately does it. Works here because Jeremy's capitulation is so seamless and fast, with no transition. The loyalty between the two characters makes it feel earned rather than lazy.

jokes.text: The old man at the party: "Next thing you know they pick me up, put me on top of this mountain and they start chanting, and I realized they thought I was God! And I'll tell you something, I thought I was too."
jokes.setup: John arrives at Claire's engagement party, blending in as a waiter; background party chatter
jokes.punchline: An old man is in the middle of a completely outrageous story — apparently being mistaken for a deity — delivered with total conviction as normal party small talk
jokes.explanation: 'I thought I was too' is a great button on a bit that only exists for 15 seconds. The confidence of an old man casually mentioning he briefly believed himself to be God at a beach club engagement party is a sharp piece of background absurdism. It's a throwaway joke that works better than many foreground ones.

jokes.text: "You!" — Sack's reaction upon seeing John at the party
jokes.setup: John has successfully infiltrated Claire's engagement party in a waiter uniform, 'ten steps ahead of Secret Service'
jokes.punchline: Sack immediately spots him — suggesting either the disguise failed instantly or Sack was specifically watching for him. The single-word 'You!' punctures John's confidence completely
jokes.explanation: The callback to John's bravado about being ahead of security pays off immediately with this. 'You!' is the simplest possible deflation of his plan. Works structurally if not brilliantly.

jokes.text: "You get near my fiancée again, I'll kill ya."
jokes.setup: Sack has confronted John at the party
jokes.punchline: His threat is genuinely delivered — no comedic inflection — which makes it funnier because he means it completely sincerely at an engagement party
jokes.explanation: Functional villain comedy. Sack's sincere death threats in polite social settings are a consistent character note. Not the strongest iteration.

jokes.text: "Did you check out the rack on that bartender? Hey, you're the Sack. She'll come to you. Oh my God, yeah, she will. You're right."
jokes.setup: Sack has just threatened to kill John and is walking away from a tense confrontation
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots to ogling the bartender — his henchman reassures him that women come to him because he's 'the Sack.' Sack is flattered and agrees: 'You're right.'
jokes.explanation: Good villain character work. Sack pivoting from murder threat to vanity within seconds, and his complete acceptance of 'you're the Sack, she'll come to you' as obvious fact, reinforces him as an oblivious alpha male. 'You're the Sack' as a reason women should be drawn to you is a small absurdist detail.

jokes.text: "About how you left me high and dry to get my ass kicked by Sack again?"
jokes.setup: Jeremy apologizes for not showing up at the party and says he wants to explain
jokes.punchline: 'Again' — implying being beaten up by Sack is now a recurring and predictable event in John's life
jokes.explanation: The word 'again' does quiet but effective work — it establishes that this has happened before and that both characters accept it as likely to keep happening. Good economy.

jokes.text: John calls Jeremy 'Judas' for falling for Gloria while also citing Rule #5
jokes.setup: Jeremy has admitted he loves Gloria and is unapologetic about it.
jokes.punchline: 'You're unbelievable! Judas! Rule #5. You're an idiot.' — John's reaction invokes both scripture and their wedding-crashing rulebook as equivalent moral authorities.
jokes.explanation: 'Judas' is funny because it's maximally dramatic for the situation. The juxtaposition of biblical betrayal with 'Rule #5' — as if the rulebook of their con operation carries similar moral weight — is the actual joke. Decent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: "There was never any rules about this. What's the rule about walking away? Never walk away on a crasher in a funny jacket. Rule #115."
jokes.setup: John invokes 'Rule #5' to condemn Jeremy for falling for a target
jokes.punchline: Jeremy counter-invokes 'Rule #115: Never walk away on a crasher in a funny jacket' — the specificity of a rule about JACKET STYLE suggests the rulebook is enormous and deeply granular
jokes.explanation: The wedding crasher rulebook is a running gag in the film, but 'Rule #115: Never walk away on a crasher in a funny jacket' is the best use of it in this reel. The specificity ('funny jacket') and the high number (115) imply this is a very elaborate, very specific canon of rules, which is funnier than a low-numbered rule would be. It's also a perfect non-sequitur that derails John's moral high ground.

jokes.text: During a child's party, apparently drunk or unhinged John shouts: 'Love doesn't exist! That's what I'm trying to tell you guys. And I'm not picking on love, 'cause I don't think friendship exists either.'
jokes.setup: John appears to be attending some kind of family/children's event, deeply depressed.
jokes.punchline: He delivers a nihilistic anti-love rant apparently TO children at a birthday party — 'you guys' implies a young audience. The equal-opportunity nihilism ('I'm not picking on love' — friendship doesn't exist either) is the kicker.
jokes.explanation: The concept of a heartbroken adult crashing a child's birthday party to announce love doesn't exist is inherently funny and character-revealing. 'I'm not picking on love' — as if he's being fair — is a nice touch. The specific addition of friendship also being fake is the escalation that makes it quotable.

jokes.text: Jeremy's speech to Gloria about being ready to take the relationship 'to the next level... to what the next level of the... of the relationship would be'
jokes.setup: Jeremy is trying to propose — apparently for the first time in his life — and cannot get the words out
jokes.punchline: His verbal mastery completely collapses; he stutters through 'the next level' three times without defining what that means
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Jeremy — the most verbally confident character in the film — completely loses his gift of gab when attempting genuine romantic sincerity. Character-specific and well-observed, but the stutter gag runs slightly long.

jokes.text: "Do you want to watch me with a girl? What about those Brazilian twins we met at the ballgame?"
jokes.setup: Jeremy says he wants to take their relationship 'to the next level' — clearly working up to a proposal
jokes.punchline: Gloria interprets 'next level' as a sexual escalation involving Brazilian twins — she's enthusiastically ready for that
jokes.explanation: Excellent character-specific misdirection. Only Gloria — established throughout the film as aggressively unhinged and sexually voracious — would hear 'I want to take our relationship to the next level' and think 'Brazilian twins.' The specificity ('Brazilian twins we met at the ballgame') implies she's been keeping them in reserve as an option, which is both funnier and more disturbing. The gap between Jeremy's nervous sincerity and Gloria's enthusiastic misinterpretation is very well-timed.

jokes.text: Before Jeremy can say 'engagement,' Gloria interrupts: 'Do you want to watch me with a girl? What about those Brazilian twins we met at the ballgame?'
jokes.setup: Jeremy is working toward the word 'engagement' in his proposal.
jokes.punchline: Gloria, apparently thinking 'next level' means something else entirely, proposes a threesome with Brazilian twins — derailing the proposal completely.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The setup is a sincere (for Jeremy) proposal attempt; the punchline is Gloria's complete misinterpretation into a sexual context — which is also, from Gloria's perspective, a sincere offer. 'The Brazilian twins we met at the ballgame' adds specificity that implies a whole offscreen history of Gloria's particular brand of unhinged generosity. Jeremy's subsequent stammer — 'that sounds terrific... that sounds unbelievable' — as he tries to hold onto the proposal is a perfect secondary beat. Character-essential: only Gloria could do this.

jokes.text: "Oh, Jeremy, I do! I love you." / "I love you." / "I-I can't believe that they're getting married."
jokes.setup: Jeremy finally manages the proposal; Gloria accepts with full enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: Cut to Secretary and Mrs. Cleary watching — the father of the bride's reaction to Gloria getting engaged to this man is 'I can't believe they're getting married.' The understatement from the person who should be most pleased is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The father's incredulity ('I can't believe they're getting married') mirrors the audience's feeling and validates it. Standard reaction comedy but well-placed.

jokes.text: "Well, we had to give her a Sweet 16 on her 13th birthday. You remember that." / "Yeah, I remember, but this is... Dad, this is marriage!" / "When you know what you want, you know what you want."
jokes.setup: Claire is alarmed that her sister Gloria is getting engaged so quickly
jokes.punchline: The father casually mentions they had to throw Gloria a Sweet 16 at age 13 — presumably because she threw a fit — and treats this as a reasonable precedent for adult marriage
jokes.explanation: The Sweet 16 at 13 detail is a perfect retroactive piece of Gloria character establishment. It reframes her entire personality — she has been this way her whole life and the family has simply capitulated repeatedly. 'When you know what you want, you know what you want' as the father's reasonable-sounding justification for enabling a grown person's every impulse is genuinely funny dark parenting comedy.

jokes.text: "Happy birthday. Can't let a little pissing and moaning break tradition. Oh right, that's today."
jokes.setup: Jeremy shows up at John's apartment with a birthday present, interrupting John's depression spiral
jokes.punchline: Jeremy acknowledges John's misery ('pissing and moaning') while still maintaining birthday tradition — and John has apparently forgotten his own birthday, suggesting his depression has made him lose track of time
jokes.explanation: 'Oh right, that's today' — John forgetting his own birthday while catastrophizing over Claire is a small, good character detail. Jeremy's matter-of-fact 'can't let a little pissing and moaning break tradition' treats John's depression with cheerful irreverence.

jokes.text: "I see you've been getting into a little light reading. That's not mine. I bought that for a friend. Yeah."
jokes.setup: Jeremy spots what appears to be a self-help or anti-suicide book at John's apartment
jokes.punchline: John immediately claims it's not his and that he 'bought it for a friend' — the most transparent possible deflection — and Jeremy's flat 'Yeah' signals complete disbelief
jokes.explanation: 'I bought that for a friend' as a denial of owning a don't-kill-yourself book is an economical dark joke. Jeremy's dry 'Yeah' is the perfect minimal response — he doesn't even bother challenging it. Good deadpan structure.

jokes.text: "Crashing weddings. Alone?" / "No, not alone. Well, who have you been crashing with then?" / "Chaz." / "Chaz?" / "Chaz." / "John, you don't even know Chaz..." / "Yes, I do."
jokes.setup: Jeremy asks what John's been up to; John claims to be 'really spectacular' and 'crashing weddings' — apparently without Jeremy
jokes.punchline: The mysterious 'Chaz' — repeated three times with increasing incredulity — implies John has scraped together a lesser crashing partner, apparently someone Jeremy doesn't believe John really knows
jokes.explanation: The 'Chaz' exchange works because of the comedic repetition structure — each echo of 'Chaz' adds disbelief. It plants a callback that pays off at the film's end, and John's dignified 'Yes, I do. He's a great guy' defensiveness about a person who is clearly not a great guy is well-played.

jokes.text: John: 'I'm hanging by a thread. I'm reading don't-kill-myself books.' Then backpedals: 'You said that the book wasn't yours.' John: 'Don't worry about the book. It isn't mine, but I glanced at it.'
jokes.setup: John has just been given good news (Jeremy is getting married) and is reacting badly because he expected sympathy.
jokes.punchline: 'Don't worry about the book. It isn't mine, but I glanced at it.' — the elaborate non-admission about the clearly-his self-help book.
jokes.explanation: 'I'm hanging by a thread. I'm reading don't-kill-myself books' is a good, dark, quick self-revelation — and then he immediately reverts to the 'it's not mine' cover. The escalation from denial to semi-admission to re-denial ('I glanced at it') is structurally satisfying.

jokes.text: "You just sat there and said that you were happy for me, that I'm... I'm hanging by a thread. I'm reading don't-kill-myself books." / "You said that the book wasn't yours." / "Don't worry about the book."
jokes.setup: John just said he was 'happy for' Jeremy's marriage news
jokes.punchline: He immediately contradicts himself — he is hanging by a thread and reading anti-suicide books. When Jeremy calls him out on denying the book, John deflects with 'don't worry about the book'
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback structure. 'Don't worry about the book' — John dismissing his own denial of a few minutes ago — is a tightly constructed joke. The callback to 'it's not mine' makes this land harder on rewatch. 'I'm hanging by a thread. I'm reading don't-kill-myself books' as a straight confession after claiming to be 'spectacular' is a perfect tonal reversal.

jokes.text: "Would mean a lot to me if you came." / "Oh, I bet it would, hillbilly." / "What?!" / "White trash!" / "What are you talking about?" / "Out! Out! You better get your ass to that wedding."
jokes.setup: Jeremy sincerely asks John to be his best man after a touching conversation about their friendship
jokes.punchline: John's response is to call Jeremy 'hillbilly' and 'white trash' and throw him out — then yell 'you better get your ass to that wedding' after him, revealing this was performative indignation and he's going
jokes.explanation: The 'hillbilly / white trash' insult sequence followed by 'you better get your ass to that wedding' is a great comedic structure for expressing begrudging love. John's pride won't let him simply say yes, so he insults Jeremy out of the apartment and then betrays his real answer through the door. The randomness of 'white trash' applied to Vince Vaughn's character is funny, and the reversal ('out! out! ...you better get to that wedding') is well-constructed.

jokes.text: "Hi, is Chaz here?" / "Chaz, there's someone here to see you!" / "Pick up your fucking skateboard!"
jokes.setup: John has been boasting about his great new crashing partner 'Chaz' throughout the conversation
jokes.punchline: John arrives at what appears to be a family home; someone shouts 'Chaz!' to summon him; Chaz is apparently a teenager or immature adult who leaves skateboards on the floor. The person shouts 'Pick up your fucking skateboard!' — immediately deflating all of John's claims about his cool new partner
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The 'Pick up your fucking skateboard!' payoff on the Chaz setup is structurally excellent — it tells us everything about Chaz in four words. John has been crashing weddings (badly, presumably) with someone whose family has to yell at him about his skateboard. The reel ends on this devastating implication about how far John has fallen. Perfect economy, earned callback, strong visual comedy implied.

jokes.text: What the fuck do you want? / God damn it, why didn't you say so? Come here, brother! Give me a hug. Bring it in for the real thing!
jokes.setup: Chaz answers with aggressive hostility — 'What the fuck do you want?'
jokes.punchline: The instant 180-degree pivot to warm, brotherly affection the moment John mentions Jeremy's name
jokes.explanation: The whiplash from aggression to warmth is a classic comedic beat, but Chaz's specific voice ('Bring it in for the real thing!') gives it genuine character specificity. Works as an effective introduction to this new, unhinged personality.

jokes.text: God damn you! I almost numbchucked you, you don't even realize.
jokes.setup: John has just sat down for a normal conversation at Chaz's place
jokes.punchline: Chaz casually reveals he nearly attacked his guest with nunchucks, treating it as a reasonable near-miss
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — the word 'numbchucked' (mispronunciation of nunchucked) and the casual delivery of a near-assault as small talk is excellent character work. Chaz is established immediately as someone who lives in a completely different reality. The specificity of the weapon and the breezy tone make this land hard.

jokes.text: Hey, Ma! Can we get some meatloaf?
jokes.setup: Chaz is a grown man who apparently lives an absurd bachelor-crasher lifestyle
jokes.punchline: He lives with his mother and casually yells to her for meatloaf mid-conversation, completely unbothered
jokes.explanation: The 'lives with Ma' detail perfectly deflates whatever dangerous mystique Chaz was building. The yell for meatloaf mid-conversation is funny in its normalcy — it becomes a running gag through the scene. Good character-building comedy.

jokes.text: What an idiot! Oh, what a loser! Good good! More for me and you.
jokes.setup: John has just told Chaz that Jeremy is getting married
jokes.punchline: Chaz's response is completely self-serving — not sympathy, not congratulations, just gleeful selfishness about having more women available
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'idiot' to 'loser' to 'more for me and you' is well-structured. Chaz's mercenary worldview is revealed instantly. The 'more for me and you' reframe of marriage as a competitive disadvantage is sharp and character-consistent.

jokes.text: I'm just living the dream!
jokes.setup: A woman has just slept with a man who lives with his mother, in a house with cartoons playing
jokes.punchline: She cheerfully announces she is 'living the dream' — maximum irony given the circumstances
jokes.explanation: Four words, enormous comedic payload. The audience sees an objectively bleak situation; she narrates it as a dream. Perfect economy. Becomes a quotable touchstone for the scene and John immediately latches onto it, which amplifies the laugh.

jokes.text: It's like I come over, I don't know what to expect... there's cartoons, your mom, and it's like, you still got it! Look at her! 'Just living the dream,' I love that!
jokes.setup: John has just witnessed the full Chaz experience — the nunchucks, the mother, the hookup leaving
jokes.punchline: John, a veteran wedding crasher himself, is genuinely impressed and disoriented, recapping the absurdity as if it were a highlight reel
jokes.explanation: John's flustered admiration works because it validates the audience's reaction. His cataloguing of absurdities ('cartoons, your mom') as evidence of success is funny. Good reaction beat that keeps the energy going.

jokes.text: Hey, Mom! The meatloaf! We want it now! The meatloaf!
jokes.setup: John has changed his mind and wants meatloaf; Chaz calls to his mother again
jokes.punchline: The escalating aggression of the meatloaf demand — 'We want it NOW! The meatloaf!' — is absurd and domineering toward his own mother
jokes.explanation: The escalation from polite request to 'WE WANT IT NOW' applied to your own mother is both absurd and weirdly recognizable. The repetition of 'The meatloaf!' as a declaration rather than a request is brilliantly unhinged. High quotability — this line has genuine cultural staying power. The running gag structure with escalation makes it funnier than the first meatloaf call.

jokes.text: What is she doing? I never know what she's doing back there.
jokes.setup: Chaz has just screamed at his mother to bring meatloaf immediately
jokes.punchline: He then muses, with genuine bafflement, about what she could possibly be doing that's taking so long
jokes.explanation: Perfect tag to the meatloaf scream — his bafflement at his own mother's slowness after yelling at her is a great character beat. The obliviousness is consistent and specific to Chaz.

jokes.text: I got her yesterday. I rode my bike over to a cemetery nearby. Her boyfriend just died.
jokes.setup: John asks where Chaz got the attractive woman who just left
jokes.punchline: Three escalating revelations: (1) he got her yesterday, (2) he rode a bike to a cemetery, (3) her boyfriend just died
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the reel. Three separate revelations stacked in rapid succession, each more shocking than the last. 'I rode my bike' introduces a pathetic image; 'to a cemetery' reframes where he met her; 'her boyfriend just died' is the dark gut-punch. The structure is near-perfect — each piece of information is funnier because of what preceded it. Pure escalation comedy with maximum economy. Chaz's casualness is essential — he treats predatory grief-harvesting as a logical lifestyle choice. Only Chaz can deliver this.

jokes.text: The dude died in a hang-gliding accident. What an idiot!
jokes.setup: John is reacting with shock to Chaz picking up a woman at her boyfriend's funeral
jokes.punchline: Chaz pivots to blaming the dead man for being an idiot who went hang-gliding
jokes.explanation: Chaz's moral compass is so skewed that he insults the dead man rather than acknowledging the predatory behavior. The hang-gliding detail is specific and absurd. 'What an idiot!' mirrors his earlier reaction to Jeremy's marriage — he applies the same judgment to marriage and accidental death, equating them, which is darkly funny.

jokes.text: 'Oh, I'm hang gliding! Honey, take a good picture... I'm dead!'
jokes.setup: Chaz has just called the dead boyfriend an idiot for hang-gliding
jokes.punchline: He performs a mock impression of the man's death, complete with cheerful photo request transitioning to death announcement
jokes.explanation: The physical impression is implied rather than read in subtitles, but the written joke structure is solid — the turn from 'take a good picture' to 'I'm dead' is a clean misdirection. Dark but earned by Chaz's character. The exclamation point delivery ('I'm dead!') as an announcement rather than a tragedy is the comedic engine.

jokes.text: Yeah, I'll throw in a wedding every now and then, but funerals are insane! The chicks are so horny, it's not even fair. It's like fishing with dynamite.
jokes.setup: John is reacting with continued disbelief to Chaz's funeral-crashing methodology
jokes.punchline: Chaz delivers a systematic defense of funeral-crashing as superior to wedding-crashing, culminating in 'fishing with dynamite'
jokes.explanation: The 'fishing with dynamite' simile is excellent — it's unexpected, perfectly captures the predatory advantage Chaz describes, and is highly quotable. The escalation from weddings to funerals as a methodological upgrade is funny in its warped logic. This is Chaz at his most conceptually sharp.

jokes.text: Grief is nature's most powerful aphrodisiac. Look it up.
jokes.setup: John is incredulous that grieving women at funerals would be 'crazy horny'
jokes.punchline: Chaz delivers a pseudo-scientific thesis with absolute authority, then tells him to 'look it up' as if it's established fact
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the reel. 'Grief is nature's most powerful aphrodisiac' works on three levels: (1) it sounds like it could be a real psychological principle; (2) it's delivered with total conviction; (3) 'Look it up' treats it as settled science. The structure is impeccable — the pseudo-authority voice perfectly captures Chaz's delusional self-confidence. Maximum economy. Highly quotable and genuinely original. This rivals the calibration anchors.

jokes.text: Ma, the meatloaf! Fuck!
jokes.setup: The meatloaf has still not arrived after multiple escalating demands
jokes.punchline: The meatloaf gag peaks with Chaz dropping an expletive at his mother mid-intellectual conversation
jokes.explanation: The final peak of the meatloaf running gag. The 'Fuck!' mid-conversation is the perfect punctuation — not directed at John, not part of any argument, just pure exasperation aimed at his own mother about meatloaf timing. Its brevity after the extended build ('The meatloaf! We want it now!') makes it hit harder by contrast. High quotability.

jokes.text: I'm not judging you, 'cause I think you're an innovator, but there's no way I'm ready for that.
jokes.setup: John is trying to decline Chaz's funeral-crashing invitation diplomatically
jokes.punchline: He calls Chaz an 'innovator' — a genuinely sincere compliment for predatory grief exploitation — before declining
jokes.explanation: John calling Chaz an 'innovator' is funny because it's a genuine business compliment applied to the most socially unacceptable possible behavior. It reveals that John is not entirely different from Chaz — just less extreme. Good character work.

jokes.text: So senseless. Damn you, Roger.
jokes.setup: An Ecclesiastes reading at a funeral is proceeding solemnly; Chaz is in the congregation
jokes.punchline: Chaz interrupts the reading with a personal, melodramatic outburst against the deceased — 'Damn you, Roger' — as if personally wronged by his death
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of solemn scripture and Chaz's personal grievance against the deceased ('Damn you, Roger') is well-executed cringe comedy. The name 'Roger' is specific enough to be funny. Chaz treats his sexual opportunity as a personal loss to be mourned dramatically. Character-consistent and surprising.

jokes.text: Roger! Damn you, Roger! Damn it! Damn you! I'm in pain. I'll try to fight it. Try to fight it. I don't know about you people, but I'm in pain.
jokes.setup: Chaz's outburst continues to escalate during the solemn funeral service
jokes.punchline: He delivers an increasingly theatrical performance of grief that is entirely about himself, culminating in the absurdly self-centered 'I don't know about you people, but I'm in pain'
jokes.explanation: 'I don't know about you people, but I'm in pain' is a brilliantly self-centered line — delivered to actual grieving people at an actual funeral, by a man who barely knew the deceased and is primarily upset about losing a sexual prospect. The escalation structure is excellent, and the line is quotable. High character integration.

jokes.text: Whoa whoa, hey! He's the best man.
jokes.setup: John arrives very late to Jeremy's wedding, apparently being physically stopped or questioned
jokes.punchline: Jeremy defends John's presence at his own wedding by announcing 'He's the best man' — as if that explains the unorthodox arrival
jokes.explanation: Functional comedic beat — the best man arriving so late he needs to be defended. Works on plot level but isn't a particularly sharp joke. The comedic payoff is primarily visual (seeing John burst in) which the transcript can't fully convey.

jokes.text: And I'm sorry I called you a hillbilly, I don't even know what that meant.
jokes.setup: John is apologizing to Gloria's family for his behavior and is listing his apologies
jokes.punchline: He apologizes for calling someone a hillbilly but undercuts it by admitting he didn't even know what the word meant when he said it
jokes.explanation: The self-undermining apology — apologizing while simultaneously making the apology worse by revealing he didn't know what he was saying — is good comic structure. The admission of ignorance about a simple insult is specifically funny.

jokes.text: Do you mind if I get married now?
jokes.setup: John and Jeremy are having an emotional reconciliation in the middle of the wedding ceremony
jokes.punchline: Jeremy cuts through the sentimentality with a dry request to actually proceed with his own wedding
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — six words that deflate the emotional moment and return focus to the absurdity of having this reconciliation at the altar. The politeness of 'Do you mind' applied to his own wedding ceremony is funny.

jokes.text: You look really pretty, by the way. That's all I'm gonna say.
jokes.setup: John is whispering to Claire during Jeremy's wedding ceremony, having promised not to bother her
jokes.punchline: He immediately compliments her appearance and then tries to close it off — 'That's all I'm gonna say' — as if one unsolicited compliment is acceptable restraint
jokes.explanation: The 'that's all I'm gonna say' self-limiting clause is immediately violated, which is good structure. The failed self-restraint is consistent with John's character and the cringe-comedy of doing this at someone else's wedding.

jokes.text: I can't stop thinking about you. It's all I think about and I don't know what to do. [Ahem.] I'm sorry.
jokes.setup: John has just said 'that's all I'm gonna say' about Claire
jokes.punchline: He immediately continues with a full confession of obsession, mid-ceremony, requiring an external cough to interrupt him
jokes.explanation: The immediate breaking of his own promise is a good structural payoff. The 'Ahem' interruption and his apology work as a cringe beat. The joke is functional but the setup pays off exactly as expected — no surprise in the subversion.

jokes.text: God, I miss you. [out loud, mid-ceremony]
jokes.setup: John has just been shushed and apologized; the ceremony continues
jokes.punchline: He cannot stop himself and blurts out another confession, escalating the cringe of his inability to maintain basic decorum
jokes.explanation: Third escalation of John's inability to stay quiet during the ceremony. Each outburst is funnier in context but diminishing returns are setting in by this point. Functional cringe escalation.

jokes.text: Oh, Jesus. It wasn't my idea. I was basically dragged to it. I went with Chaz, who you forgot to tell me is totally insane.
jokes.setup: John is mid-romantic speech to Claire and has just mentioned he crashed a funeral
jokes.punchline: His explanation — 'I was basically dragged to it' and 'Chaz, who you forgot to tell me is totally insane' — is a defensive digression that undercuts his romantic speech
jokes.explanation: The pivot from romantic confession to defensive explanation about Chaz is a good structural choice — it deflates the speech's sentimentality right at the moment of maximum vulnerability. 'Who you forgot to tell me is totally insane' is a funny blame-shift.

jokes.text: He also might be a genius because it actually does work. He's cleaning up.
jokes.setup: John has just called Chaz 'totally insane' in the middle of his romantic speech to Claire
jokes.punchline: He immediately qualifies it by endorsing Chaz's methodology as effective — 'He's cleaning up' — mid-love-speech, mid-wedding
jokes.explanation: This is the best line of John's speech — the fact that he can't resist defending and even praising Chaz's funeral-crashing during a sincere romantic monologue reveals that John hasn't entirely changed. 'He's cleaning up' as an assessment of grief exploitation is darkly funny. The self-correction that follows ('I'm sorry, that's neither here nor there') is good structure.

jokes.text: This congregation really doesn't care about how depressing your life is, John, okay?
jokes.setup: John has just delivered a lengthy, emotional speech at Claire's wedding — right in front of her fiancé
jokes.punchline: Sack's response dismisses the entire emotional plea as merely 'depressing' and appeals to the congregation's comfort
jokes.explanation: Sack as the antagonist gets a solid line here — characterizing the romantic speech as simply 'depressing' and deploying the congregation as social pressure is consistent with his character as a bully who operates through social hierarchy. Good economy.

jokes.text: Sack, I've always liked you... so I put up with your stories about scallops and otters, and it's all good because you seemed to make her happy.
jokes.setup: The father of the bride is addressing Sack after Claire refuses to marry him
jokes.punchline: His expression of tolerance for Sack is 'I put up with your stories about scallops and otters' — an absurdly specific detail that implies Sack is an insufferable bore
jokes.explanation: 'Scallops and otters' is a brilliantly specific comedic detail — it implies a whole world of boring Sack dinner party anecdotes without explaining them. The father's diplomatic framing of tolerance ('it's all good') followed by this specific grievance is sharp. The specificity is what elevates this from generic 'you're annoying' to something genuinely funny.

jokes.text: Wow, getting a nice preview of what marriage is gonna be like with Ike Turner here.
jokes.setup: Sack has just screamed a crude command at Claire in front of the entire congregation
jokes.punchline: John compares Sack to Ike Turner — the famously abusive musician — framing Sack's behavior as a preview of domestic violence
jokes.explanation: The Ike Turner reference is a pop culture name-drop that works modestly — the comparison is apt given Sack's behavior. 'Nice preview' as the frame is clever. However, it's a dated reference and the joke structure is fairly predictable (bad behavior + famous abuser comparison). Functional but not particularly sharp.

jokes.text: Share that with the Dalai Lama, jackass.
jokes.setup: John has just made the Ike Turner crack; Sack responds
jokes.punchline: Sack's comeback — 'Share that with the Dalai Lama, jackass' — is a non-sequitur insult that makes no logical sense but is delivered with aggression
jokes.explanation: The Dalai Lama reference as a comeback is funny precisely because it makes no sense — it's what an aggressive idiot says when he wants to sound smart and fails. The 'jackass' tag is a good deflation. The absurdity of the non-sequitur is the joke.

jokes.text: I think I had him. / I know you did. Just go kiss the broad.
jokes.setup: John and Sack have just had a confrontation; John apparently landed a punch or won the exchange physically
jokes.punchline: John's self-assessment ('I think I had him') and Jeremy's pragmatic validation followed by 'just go kiss the broad' deflates the testosterone moment instantly
jokes.explanation: 'Just go kiss the broad' is good — it cuts through the male posturing with blunt pragmatism. The 'broad' usage is period-appropriate and funny coming from Jeremy in this context. Good economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Would it be a total cliché if I kissed you right now? / Yes.
jokes.setup: John is about to kiss Claire in a classic romantic-comedy finale moment
jokes.punchline: He meta-acknowledges the cliché; she confirms it is; they kiss anyway
jokes.explanation: A clever bit of meta-commentary that earns its climax. The question is self-aware, her answer is perfect deadpan ('Yes'), and the act of doing it anyway is what makes the moment both romantic and funny. Maximum economy — four words is all it takes. The structure is tight: setup, honest confirmation, subversion through action. Well above average for a climactic kiss joke.

jokes.text: With every death there comes rebirth. It's the circle of life. We're gonna be all right.
jokes.setup: The wedding chaos has resolved; Chaz appears to deliver pseudo-wisdom
jokes.punchline: Chaz appropriates funeral/grief philosophy to comment on a wedding situation, treating all life events as interchangeable through his warped lens
jokes.explanation: Chaz delivering life-philosophy at a wedding that nearly became a funeral is consistent character work. 'We're gonna be all right' as his benediction is funny given his worldview. Solid but not among his best lines.

jokes.text: So, what's next? / I'm starving. / Fujimora wedding, 3:00 P.M. / They would have great tempura.
jokes.setup: The romantic resolution has just occurred; everyone is basking in the happy ending
jokes.punchline: The couples immediately pivot to crashing the next wedding — with the food as the primary motivation — suggesting nothing has fundamentally changed
jokes.explanation: A genuinely satisfying comedic button on the entire film. The fact that they're immediately back to crashing weddings — even after all the character growth — and that the girls are IN on it, and that the hook is 'great tempura,' is a perfect landing. 'We don't even have a back story' followed by 'We're a folk-singing group from Salt Lake City!' captures the impulsive joy of the crashing lifestyle. High craft for a closing gag.

jokes.text: Jeremy trying to hug/approach someone and being physically restrained — 'Hey. Uh-uh-uh. Hey. Uh-uh!'
jokes.setup: In the aftermath of the wedding chaos, Jeremy apparently tries to embrace or approach someone.
jokes.punchline: He is physically stopped — twice — with the universal 'uh-uh' sound of denial, implying his enthusiasm is both excessive and unwelcome.
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy inferred from dialogue sounds. Without the visual it's hard to fully evaluate, but the repeated denial reads as a mild sight gag. Functional, not distinctive.

jokes.text: We don't even have a back story, I just... / No, forget it, forget it. / I'm talking out loud.
jokes.setup: John has semi-seriously suggested crashing the Fujimora wedding
jokes.punchline: He catches himself — 'I'm talking out loud' — acknowledging he's reverted to crash-planning mode without meaning to
jokes.explanation: Good transitional beat — John's self-awareness about reverting to type is funny. 'I'm talking out loud' is a nice, economical self-catch. Functional character moment.

jokes.text: We're a folk-singing group from Salt Lake City! / Yes we are.
jokes.setup: The group has been tentatively considering crashing the Fujimora wedding without a back story
jokes.punchline: Gloria immediately invents a complete cover story with no hesitation; Jeremy enthusiastically confirms it
jokes.explanation: Gloria instantly producing 'folk-singing group from Salt Lake City' is funny for its specificity — not just folk singers, but from Salt Lake City. Jeremy's instant 'Yes we are!' without a beat of hesitation shows complete buy-in. The girls being as eager as the boys to crash is a satisfying character payoff. Good economy and energy.
